item.title: A Document-Borne AI Worm in Copilot for Word
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

Håkon Måløy, writing on En Klype Salt, reports that hidden instructions inside a Word document can survive a Copilot drafting session and end up inside the document it produces. That document then contains the same instructions, so the next person who uses it as source material gets the same treatment. This is the third part of a series on Copilot and untrusted input, after Poisoning Copilot Memory and When Emails Instruct. Both of those were fixed. The vulnerability here was not: coordination with Microsoft’s Security Response Center ran 144 days, Microsoft closed each specific payload reported, and the class was still reproducible at publication.

The write-up walks through each stage with screenshots. The outline:

  • The payload. The attack starts as a prompt in JSON format appended to an otherwise ordinary document, set in white text at a small size. Copilot for Word strips color and font size before the text reaches the model, so the model reads what the person cannot see. The post calls this a cross-domain prompt injection attack (XPIA), a variant of prompt injection where the instructions arrive with content pulled in from outside the current task.
  • Stage one, the first document. With the malicious file among the attachments, Copilot follows the embedded instructions while drafting and says nothing about having done so. Copilot also reaches the file without being pointed at it, by searching the victim’s OneDrive for relevant source material.
  • Stage two, propagation. The instructions also tell Copilot to copy them into the document it writes, again in white text. That document is now an internal file, and it is trusted as one, so attaching it in a later drafting session triggers the attack again, with the attacker’s original document no longer among the attachments.
  • Why it is still open. Rewording a closed payload reproduced the whole chain, because the class is the mechanism rather than any particular prompt. The post’s argument is that a model has to read untrusted text in order to judge whether it is an attack, and by then that text is already part of the computation that produces the judgment. The one control it asks for is provenance metadata recording source material and model edits, which would make the spread traceable without preventing it. The post also flags Copilot’s integration with Microsoft Cowork and Microsoft Scout, which create and edit documents automatically, as a path for the same mechanism to spread at machine speed.

My Notes

  • Someone has to reuse the document: a person attaches the affected file, or asks for a report that sends Copilot looking for source material. Morris II, the email-assistant worm the post cites as precedent, did not need that. It poisoned the databases those assistants search, and they read mail without being asked. So this spreads at whatever rate people reuse each other’s documents. That is slower than a worm that moves on its own. It is also harder to spot, since every step is a person doing ordinary work.
  • Copilot is not the attacker here: Tracebit’s context bombs cut attack success by roughly 90% by planting text that an attacking model refuses to work alongside. That defense assumes the model is doing something its safety training objects to. This attack instead has Copilot edit numbers in a report it was already asked to draft, which is not the kind of instruction a model refuses.

Related Posts

  • Context Bombs: Stopping AI Attackers in Their Tracks: prompt injection planted by the defender to stop an attacking model, a defense that does not reach an attack whose payload is ordinary business editing.
  • Prompt Injections in the Wild: What Google Found in Common Crawl: Google’s census of injections on the public web found mostly low-effort experiments, a different population from a coordinated disclosure against a shipped product.
  • Snowflake Cortex AI Escapes Sandbox and Executes Malware: the same untrusted-content-as-instruction failure aimed at code execution rather than at the contents of a document.
  • Indirect Prompt Injection Threats: the 2023 demonstration that planted text can redirect an assistant, three years before the same mechanism reached a mainstream productivity suite.

item.title: Jeff Dean: Important Trends in AI
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

Jeff Dean, Chief Scientist for Google Research and Google DeepMind and a co-lead of Gemini, gave the Princeton CS Distinguished Colloquium on February 10, 2026. His title was “Important Trends in AI: How Did We Get Here, What Can We Do Now, and Where are We Headed?” The talk runs 78 minutes. About 40 of them are a chronological tour of the advances that produced current models, most of which he either worked on or sat next to. The rest is Gemini, the logistics of a thousand-author project, and four audience questions.

Six months after this talk, on August 5, 2026, Dean announced he was leaving Google after almost 27 years. He is now CEO of Discovery Loop, a public benefit corporation set up to automate the scientific method itself across chip design, biology, drug discovery, and material design. Three colleagues left with him: Sanjay Ghemawat, his collaborator on much of Google’s core infrastructure, plus Oriol Vinyals and Quoc Le, two of the three researchers he credits by name in this lecture for the sequence-to-sequence work. Google took a stake and agreed to supply compute for the first year.

The talk, in brief:

  • Scale and architecture multiply rather than add. His summary of the last 13 or 14 years: 20× from scale times 50× from better architectures is a thousand-fold improvement, and both terms have kept delivering.
  • His 1990 undergraduate thesis was model-parallel and data-parallel training, under the names “pattern partitioned” and “pipelined.” The speedup curves tapered off because he held the model size fixed while adding processors, and he then left the subject alone for 25 years.
  • The TPU program started from one back-of-envelope calculation: a billion users talking to a good speech model three minutes a day would have required doubling the number of computers Google had.
  • Silent data corruption is treated as a first-class training problem, with per-layer gradient-norm monitoring, automatically triggered deterministic replay to separate bad hardware from bad batches, and hot spares swapped into a synchronous job mid-run.
  • Gemini’s IMO gold medal came with more specialization than the talk describes. It solved five of six problems. The public record adds reinforcement-learning training on multi-step reasoning data, a corpus of high-quality solutions, and IMO-specific instructions, while the talk describes an out-of-the-box model given a large thinking budget.
  • Inference efficiency is where he expects the next gains, along with attending to a trillion tokens through learned retrieval instead of a larger context window.
  • Slope beats absolute score in his answer to an audience member who asked what to do with a thousand TPUs. Run the same idea at three tiny sizes and read the trend: an idea below the baseline with a good slope is more interesting than one that starts above it and decays.

The video has no chapter markers, so the enriched transcript at the bottom of this post has its own outline: 11 sections and 61 topic subsections, each section linking to its YouTube timestamp. It also adds hyperlinks on first mention, bracketed acronym expansions, and editor’s notes on the handful of claims worth checking. The outline is in the right-hand sidebar.

Dean presents slides throughout, and the audio alone does not always say what is on them. 65 slides are captured below, each placed near the point in the transcript where he speaks to it and captioned with a link to that moment in the video. The Q&A has none, since the camera stays on the room.

Section outline (jump to the enriched transcript below, or watch on YouTube):

  • 0:00:12 — Introduction (YouTube)
  • 0:02:56 — Four observations about where AI is (YouTube)
  • 0:05:00 — Neural nets, backpropagation, and a 1990 undergraduate thesis (YouTube)
  • 0:08:00 — Scaling up: DistBelief, word2vec, seq2seq, and the first TPUs (YouTube)
  • 0:22:30 — Transformers, sparsity, and the training substrate (YouTube)
  • 0:36:15 — Chain of thought, distillation, RL, and speculative decoding (YouTube)
  • 0:47:20 — Gemini (YouTube)
  • 1:01:20 — Organizing a thousand-author effort (YouTube)
  • 1:05:30 — Where this is headed (YouTube)
  • 1:08:35 — Shaping AI, and conclusion (YouTube)
  • 1:11:25 — Audience Q&A (YouTube)

Transcript

Built from the talk’s YouTube auto-captions. Section boundaries, topic subsections, punctuation, capitalization, and paragraph breaks are all editorial: the video ships without chapter markers and auto-captions arrive without punctuation. Fillers, repeated words, and false starts are trimmed, so this is lightly edited rather than strictly verbatim, but nothing is paraphrased, summarized, or reordered. Caption mishearings of names and technical terms are fixed silently (Andrew Ng, Ilya Sutskever, Oriol Vinyals, Quoc Le, ImageNet, ISCA, HBM, JAX, LMArena, GSM8K, Nano Banana, bonza, LiDAR, Waymo, CACM, processors), and one award name too garbled to recover is reconstructed in brackets. Speaker labels appear in the introduction and the Q&A. The lecture body is one speaker, so it has none.

0:00:12 — Introduction

Kai Li: Good afternoon. It’s not 4:30 yet, but since the room is already full, I’ll just start doing introduction to save some time. Okay. It’s a real pleasure to introduce Jeff Dean, a chief scientist for Google Research and the Google DeepMind, and also he’s a co-lead of Gemini project.

I would say before the now famous Jeff Dean at Google era, I actually met Jeff in the 90s when Jeff was in Digital Western Research, and so I can confirm is not overnight success story. Jeff has been quietly exceptional for a very long time.

Jeff’s bio you probably read in the flyer reads a little bit like a guided tour of modern computing, from large-scale information retrieval, operating system, distributed system, compilers. And then if that wasn’t enough, the second career is that AI machine, you know, ML accelerator, vision model, low-level software — I’m going to not upgrade Chrome right now [laughter] — and also distillation, neural network architecture search, large language multimodal model, and application ranging from chip design to healthcare, translation, and so on.

So one of my favorite details of Jeff is that he did his undergraduate thesis on neural networks, and which means two things I think. First, he worked on neural network before it was cool. And second, he has the rare distinction being able to say I like neural network before Google made it popular. Okay, maybe Jeff did that to himself.

But if you’re wondering what takes to be good, to have a good research taste, apparently the answer is start early to be Jeff. So along the way Jeff has received the ACM Prize in Computing, [IEEE John von Neumann] Medal. He’s a ACM fellow, a member of US National Academy of Engineering and American Academy of Arts and Sciences.

Note

Editor’s note. The award name after the ACM Prize in Computing is garbled beyond recovery in the captions (“ite medal”), and the bracketed reconstruction above is inferred from Dean’s actual award record rather than heard: he received the IEEE John von Neumann Medal in 2021 and the ACM Prize in Computing in 2012.

0:02:56 — Four observations about where AI is

Kai Li: So, we’re very fortunate to have him to give us the distinguished lecture today. Please join me to welcome Jeff.

Jeff Dean: All right. [applause] Thank you very much for that kind introduction and for hosting me. I’m unexpectedly in town and Kai said, “Hey, you want to come by and give a talk?” So, I’m delighted to be here.

And I’m going to talk to you about what’s happening in AI. I don’t know if you’ve noticed, but it’s a thing these days. And we have many people at Google working on this area. So, I’m presenting the work of not just my work, but many, many people at Google and elsewhere.

Computers can now see, hear, and read

So, a few observations which may not come as a huge surprise to you. So machine learning and AI have really changed our expectations of what is possible with computers. You know, if you think back 10, 15 years ago, computers couldn’t see very well. They couldn’t really understand speech all that well. They definitely couldn’t understand language very well.

And now we have tools that enable computers to interact with people in a much more natural style because they understand the modalities that people understand and want to communicate with.

Scale times algorithms: 20× and 50× make 1000×

And along the way, increasing scale of larger amounts of compute, larger amounts of data, and more larger scale models have delivered better results nearly continuously for the last sort of 13 or 14 years. This has been the trend and seems to be holding up even today.

In addition to scale, algorithmic and sort of model architecture improvements have also provided massive improvements as well. And these two things multiply together, right? If you can have much larger scale and much better model architectures that are able to learn more per floating point operation, those things together mean instead of 20x from scale, you have 20x from scale and 50x from algorithms and you end up with a thousandx better thing than you had not that long ago.

0:05:00 — Neural nets, backpropagation, and a 1990 undergraduate thesis

Also, the kinds of computations we want to run and the hardware in which we want to run them are changing dramatically.

So four observations which are maybe not surprising. First, neural nets and gradient descent. These seem to be key building blocks for how do you actually build truly intelligent computer systems.

Not new ideas: the 70s, the 80s, and an intro lecture in 1990

And they’re not new ideas. They’re things that have been around for a long time. They were invented in the 70s and 80s. And there was actually a lot of excitement about them in the late 80s and early 90s.

I first ran across them in an intro lecture where I was introduced to neural networks roughly like this. You know, we have this kind of nice very abstracted away version of how we think real life neurons behave, where you have a bunch of inputs, you do some processing, and you decide are you going to fire or not, and what strength are you going to fire, and you have connections of these things.

And then back propagation is a really nice algorithm that enables you to adjust the weights on the edges of all these connections in order to make the model behave more in the way that you want it to behave, where you give it a bunch of examples and back propagation enables you to make the model learn the behavior you want.

So I saw these as an undergrad in 1990 and I got super excited and I said, “Oh wow, that seems like a really good abstraction. It feels like it’s a trainable thing and it can learn almost anything.”

A senior thesis that was model parallelism and data parallelism

And at that time we were not using very large neural networks because we had really pathetically wimpy computers. But I said, “Oh, maybe if we use the parallel computer in the department, we could train much bigger neural networks. That would be great. Maybe we just need to use 32 computers instead of one and then we could train really impressive neural nets. That would be nice.”

So, I did it. I asked the professor who introduced the neural networks topic in one of the classes I was taking if I could do a senior thesis with him, Vipin Kumar. And he said, “Sure.”

So I played around with two different approaches for training neural networks in parallel. One is this is what you would now call model parallel and data parallel training. But I called them pattern partitioned and pipelined approach.

And these speed up curves are interesting but they taper off because I did the stupid thing. I didn’t make the model bigger and bigger as I increase the number of processors. I just made it much harder to parallelize with a fixed size model.

But I sort of filed that away as like, oh, that’s an interesting abstraction and it seems like something I should pay attention to. But then I ignored it for the next 25 years.

0:08:00 — Scaling up: DistBelief, word2vec, seq2seq, and the first TPUs

Okay. So now I’m going to give you a whirlwind tour of a bunch of advances in the field of ML that have happened in the last 15 years that are really all combined together to produce today’s most sophisticated models. How did these today’s models come to be? Well, it was through advancements like the ones I’m going to describe.

Bumping into Andrew Ng in a micro kitchen

So, the origin of my getting back to working on neural nets at Google was I bumped into Andrew Ng, who’s a Stanford faculty member, in one of our micro kitchens and I said, “Oh, what are you doing here?” He’s like, “I’m not sure yet, because I just started a week ago. But my students at Stanford are doing interesting things with training neural networks for speech and vision.”

I’m like, “Oh, that’s cool. We should train really big neural networks,” because we actually had quite a lot of computers in those days. And I said, “Oh, why don’t we try training very, very large neural networks?”

Asynchronous replicas and parameter servers: “theoretically wrong” but it worked

And so we built a software system [1] that enabled us to express neural network and connectivity of those neural networks and do both model and data parallel training across many, many computers. And that enabled us to train neural networks that were 50 to 100 times larger than the largest ones we could find anyone talking about.

And we had a way of doing this where we had actually many, many asynchronous replicas of the model getting updates of what the current parameters of the model were, churning away on their local batch of examples, computing a gradient and sending it to this distributed set of parameter servers in order to update the parameters of the model.

This is, because it’s asynchronous, definitely not the right mathematical thing, because in the meantime the model parameters have moved from the other replicas giving the parameter servers updates to the parameters. But it seemed to work, so we were sort of happy anyway despite it being sort of theoretically wrong.

Cat neurons from 10 million unlabeled YouTube frames

And one of the first things we trained was a very large model to do completely unsupervised learning [2] on 10 million random YouTube frames. And interestingly, we had a kind of a locally connected neural network for computer vision that would use a reconstruction loss.

So we try to take a high level representation of the neurons at the highest level of the model and then try to reconstruct the pixels that have been given as input, and because that bottleneck layer forced the model to sort of learn higher level abstractions than the actual raw pixels.

What we ended up finding was at the top level of this model, some of the neurons had learned to be sensitive to whether or not there was a face of a cat in the image. Some of them learned to be sensitive to whether there was a face. Some were sensitive to, you know, is this the outline of a person. All without being told any of these images contained any of those kinds of objects. So it’s kind of neat to see that you could learn these high level abstractions and representations from a purely unsupervised objective.

A 70% relative improvement on ImageNet 22k

What we could then do is use the initialization of this unsupervised training in order to train with a supervised method to try to do computer vision image classification. And we used, unfortunately we used, the 22,000 category version of ImageNet, which is a more thinly traded version than the 1000 category one that most people are most familiar with.

But we got a 70% relative improvement in ImageNet 22k state-of-the-art by initializing with our unsupervised model and then doing supervised learning on the training set for that data set, which is quite a large relative improvement. So we were happy with that and we saw that scale really mattered.

word2vec: nearby words cluster, and directions mean something

We also started to do a bunch of work in using neural networks for language tasks. And one of the things we found was that even relatively simple models where you have a vector-based representation of words or phrases [3], so that you have a nice thousand or 500 dimensional representation of each word or token, and have relatively shallow models.

So in fact we had just the embedding vector, and then we would use the embedding vector of the word to try to predict nearby words. That was one of the approaches we tried.

And what we found was that if you apply this to lots of text and use this training objective, you end up with nearby words in the high-dimensional space tend to be related ones. So like cat and puma and tiger are all low distance in the high-dimensional space. And also that directions are meaningful. So you go in the same direction to change the gender of a word in a gendered language regardless of what word you start with. King and queen.

seq2seq: an LSTM encoder’s final state as the decoder’s initial state

A year or two later, three of my colleagues Ilya Sutskever, Oriol Vinyals and Quoc Le used a neural encoder [4] using an LSTM [long short-term memory] to essentially be able to learn an encoder for one sequence and then a decoder for a different sequence.

And when you initialize the state of the LSTM by running the encoder, that ends up sort of capturing the things that have occurred in that input sequence and enables the model to then use that initial state to then do a good job of predicting the target sequence.

So the canonical example use case of this is language translation, where maybe you have a bunch of English-French sentence pairs that mean the same thing and the input sentence is English. And so when you’re training you try to decode the French sentence and you get a supervised learning objective for every token or for every word. And then when you’re trying to translate a new sentence you just use the encoder to encode the LSTM state and then decode from that state in order to produce the translated French.

The back-of-envelope calculation that started the TPU program

So as we saw more and more success of neural networks, and in particular scaling up neural networks for problems in computer vision, speech recognition and language, we were starting to both get excited but also a bit worried about how we would actually deploy these much better models.

So this is kind of the origin of how we started to create our own tensor processing unit chip program. I did this back of the envelope calculation and said, okay, we have this really nice high quality speech recognition model. It has the error rate for speech recognition which is a huge improvement. It’s sort of equivalent to 20 years of speech research in like six months since we started the project, by training just a very large, not particularly sophisticated model architecture. It’s like an eight layer fully connected neural net just trained on a lot of data.

And that back of the envelope calculation said if we wanted to deploy this to a scenario where we had a billion users talking to this model 3 minutes a day, we would need to double the number of computers Google had. And that didn’t seem very tenable for rolling out a better speech recognition system.

So that really convinced us that exploring much more specialized computational devices for doing neural network inference and later neural network training was going to be a fruitful path. And so this sort of bootstrap got us to really approach that with conviction and started up a chip design team in order to build these chips.

TPUv1: reduced precision and a handful of linear-algebra operations

And then the first chip emerged two years later, as hardware projects tend to do. They take a little while, but we eventually produced the TPUv1 chip [5], which took advantage of two really nice properties of neural networks.

The first is that reduced precision is fine, especially for inference. So you’re perfectly happy with about seven or eight bits of precision, not 16 or 32 or 64 as most people are thinking about in terms of floating-point computation things.

And also that nearly all of the models we were exploring were made up of different combinations of a handful of specific kinds of linear algebra operations. You know, things like matrix multiplies are at the heart of them, and then certain kinds of dot products and normalization and scaling.

But if you think about most of the machine learning algorithms of today, different rearrangements of those kinds of operations mean that you can build an accelerator that is capable of very high performance reduced precision linear algebra and that can be applicable to a pretty wide range of neural networks. And it’s much more efficient because that’s all it needs to do. It doesn’t need to do anything else. It doesn’t need to run Microsoft Word or Chrome or anything else.

And so TPUv1 turned out to be 15 to 30x faster than contemporary CPUs and GPUs and 30 to 80 times more energy efficient than contemporary CPUs and GPUs. And it’s also now the most cited paper in ISCA’s [International Symposium on Computer Architecture] 50-year history.

Optical interconnect and racks you can swap mid-run

So we then turned the chip design team’s attention to the training problem, because we felt like being able to scale up training more than we were able to on CPUs and GPUs was going to be important. And so this is where the focus has been for quite a while.

And we’ve now produced many, many generations of TPUs that are essentially machine learning supercomputers, right? It’s more than just a single chip, unlike TPUv1. Instead it’s lots and lots of chips connected with a custom high-speed interconnect that enables us to distribute model training over those chips and communicate both activations and parameter updates and gradient updates across that custom interconnect.

Version four introduced this funky thing where we have an optical interconnect for racks of these accelerators. So, there’s a rack of 64 accelerators and we can make it seem as though that rack of 64 accelerators is right next to another rack of 64 accelerators even though they’re 100 meters across the data center floor.

And if that rack fails, we can swap in another rack and make it seem as though this rack is now right next to that one in terms of the net topology. Which is important. As you get more and more scale, you end up with failures. And so you want to be able to reconfigure things like that.

Reading the generation table: TPUv4 to Ironwood

And so we’ve seen continual hardware performance scaling. So if you look at TPUv4 here on the left column, the peak flops per chip is about 275 teraflops. The max pod size was 4,896 chips, and now we’re sort of at roughly double that pod size and much, much more HBM [high-bandwidth memory] and much more memory bandwidth and many more flops per chip.

Note

Editor’s note. Two things about that table. Ironwood is Google’s seventh-generation TPU: the sixth is Trillium, announced at Google I/O in May 2024 and generally available that December, and it is the generation the table skips, going v5p straight to Ironwood. Dean flags the numbering as confusing in the same breath, since Google dropped the “v7” branding for Ironwood. Separately, the TPU v4 pod size shown as 4,896 is documented by Google as 4,096 chips, and the TPU v4 paper cited on Dean’s own earlier slide also gives 4,096. The transcript reproduces the figure he read off the slide.

If you compare the peak performance per pod, which is sort of the largest network configuration we have of the custom interconnect, the TPUv2 pod is 1x and the most recent sort of v6 — but now we’ve stopped numbering them, sadly, it’s harder to keep track of, but Ironwood is the sixth generation of TPUs — is about 3600 times the performance per pod of TPUv2. And it’s also much more energy efficient, so about 30x better flops per watt, which is what you ultimately care about.

TensorFlow, PyTorch, and JAX

The other thing that has happened in the last 15 years is open source tools have really enabled the whole community to build using the same pieces of abstraction and software libraries, and the community can work on sort of improving those tools as well.

So we developed a software called TensorFlow based on our initial lessons from the sort of 2011 to 2014 era with an internal software library that we were using to parallelize computations across many computers and train large models and do inference.

And then more recently various people at Meta and elsewhere introduced PyTorch, and then another group of people at Google have introduced a more functional style paradigm computation called JAX. All of these are great systems, and we have been using JAX for our Gemini training and it’s been great.

0:22:30 — Transformers, sparsity, and the training substrate

Why LSTMs don’t parallelize: one state update per token

And then in 2017 a number of my colleagues worked on coming up with a better architecture [6] than the sort of recurrent LSTMs that were kind of the state-of-the-art models for language at the time.

And the observation they had was really, in an LSTM you have a vector of state of sort of the current representation of the state, and then when you advance one token at a time you update that state, and there’s a sophisticated thing that updates the state, and then you go on to the next word and you update the state again. And so as you progress through say a hundred words of a sentence you update the state a 100 times.

And there’s two problems with that. One is you have this sequential process. Every word you have to wait for the update of the state, and there’s a sequential dependency on that state being ready before you can go on to update the state for the next word. So, it’s not very parallelizable, which is not good on modern hardware.

And the other thing is you’re trying to force all the things you went through into a single vector, that you have all the things you might want to remember from the things you went through in a single vector, rather than just saving all the vectors you went through and then being able to look at them as you wish later in the sort of language modeling process.

Save the vectors and learn where to look

So the key observation in the transformer model is let’s save all those vectors, or some representation of those vectors, and then pay attention to them in a way where we have a learnable attention mechanism.

And what they were able to show was that compared to LSTMs of one, two or four layers in red there, the test loss on the y-axis went down considerably using a transformer, and no matter what model scale you looked at. So sort of 10 to 100x less compute and 10 times smaller model gave you with a transformer roughly the same quality as you would get with an LSTM that’s much larger.

Self-supervised learning: there is a lot of text in the world

In 2018, I think people really started to take seriously the idea, well, I guess in the word2vec work we were already sort of doing that, but in 2018, really looking at how could you do language modeling at scale with self-supervised data. And just the observation there’s a lot of text in the world.

And so self-supervised learning on this text can give you almost unlimited amounts of training data where you know the right answer, right? Like you have text and then you hide the next word and you try to guess the next word, and if you guess it correctly that gives you a sort of a one, and if you guess it wrong that gives you a clear error signal that you can propagate into improving the model, so that in such settings you will guess better next time. And so this is really one of the major reasons that these chat and language models have gotten so good.

Autoregressive against fill-in-the-blank

And so there are two kinds of training objectives that people typically use. One is called autoregressive, where you get to look at the prefix, everything to the left, and try to predict the next word. So “Princeton blank,” you know, that word is a little bit hard to predict. Could be Princeton New Jersey, could be Princeton University. “Princeton University blank.” That one’s hard to predict as well. “Is cold in the blank,” that one’s a little easier to predict. So that’s autoregressive.

And then fill in the blank [7] is where you get to have a training objective where you just hide, you get to look in both directions and you hide some of the words and you try to force the model to guess the missing words that you’ve hidden. And every so often we incorporate say successful experiments demonstrated at larger scale into a new candidate baseline and then we repeat. And that seems to have worked pretty well.

1:05:30 — Where this is headed

Managing a team of 50 virtual assistants

Sorry, a few forward-looking thoughts. I mean I think one area that’s going to be really important is how do humans and AI agents collaborate to get stuff done, right? Like currently a lot of the uses of these models are you have a single person sitting down with an interactive chatbot interface doing stuff.

But in the future it seems like more work is going to happen where the human is coordinating the activities of a dozen or hundred AI agents doing stuff on their behalf, where the human has probably weakly specified what it is they want. How can we give the right HCI [human-computer interaction] paradigm for managing a team of 50 of these virtual assistants? How can the agents themselves cooperate to accomplish things? What will this enable? I think these are all pretty interesting directions.

A trillion tokens instead of a million

I think the million tokens of context is quite useful, and that gives you a thousand pages of text or hours of video or whatever. But it seems like it’d be even more useful to be able to attend to a trillion tokens of stuff rather than a million.

And so I think hybrid systems with learned retrieval algorithms over large corpora, and then maybe lightweight models that can be used to assess how relevant are these 30,000 documents I retrieved to the thing I’m trying to do, and then put the maybe hundred things you actually think are really, really important into the context window. And maybe precomputation from a computer systems perspective to make this all efficient and fast.

I think there’d be a lot of uses for this. Personalized Gemini. I’d love it if I could attend to all of my email state and photos and so on, with my permission of course. Web search, multimodal search and retrieval, like searching all the YouTube videos. Coding agents, like every coding agent at Google, it’d be nice if it attended to the whole Google codebase for every Google developer.

Inference efficiency, and using AI to design the chips

And then forward-looking, I think inference efficiency is going to be really critical, right? Like the training cost of these models is very large and you need a lot of chips. But going forward more and more inference is going to happen, and more and more agents using these things in sophisticated ways and interacting with other agents that themselves are doing inference.

So specialized hardware designed purely for inference is going to be important. Again, I think model and algorithmic improvements for efficient inference are going to be important. Low latency for these inference cases is a huge plus. It’s just much more enjoyable to use something that responds in 100 milliseconds than 5 seconds.

And I believe in the future that AI applied to automating chip design [20] is going to be one of the ways in which we get much more efficient inference hardware. I have a whole talk on this, but essentially it’s use learning as much as possible, and RL.

1:08:35 — Shaping AI, and conclusion

Seven domains, and a paper with its own website

Okay. I have, sorry I’m running over, I have two more slides here. One of the other things that we did in the last couple years is we got together a group of co-authors thinking about what are the impacts of AI in many different domains of the world [21], not just computer science. And we wanted to look at what these impacts might be, both positive and negative.

And so we identified seven domains we thought would be pretty dramatically impacted by AI. So employment, education, healthcare, misinformation, media, entertainment, governance and national security, and AI for science. And then we went out and we interviewed a bunch of domain experts in these areas, and in particular tried to find people we thought would have interesting perspectives on one or more of these domain areas. And then we wrote up what we learned from chatting with the domain experts as well as our own thoughts.

And so we produced a long arXiv paper which not that many people have read. So we have a shorter version in CACM, and Dave Patterson, one of the co-authors, wrote a nice one-page editorial on the Economist. And this is all available on shapingai.com. I think this is a pretty interesting paper. I think it has some good insights into what will the impact of AI beyond say employment and technology transitions. As one example, it’s the only paper I have with its own website.

Conclusion

Okay. In conclusion, I think AI models like Gemini and products built with them are becoming really important and powerful tools for the things we try to do every day. Further research and innovation is going to continue this trend. It’s going to have a dramatic impact in many of the areas that I just mentioned in the Shaping AI paper, healthcare, education, science, all kinds of things.

It potentially makes really deep expertise, like these models are really good in some areas, and it makes that available to many people all over the world, which is a pretty powerful capability. And done well, I think our AI assisted future is going to be really bright. All right.

1:11:25 — Audience Q&A

“What’s your biggest fear about AI?”

Audience member: What’s your biggest fear about AI?

Jeff Dean: My biggest fear of AI? I mean, I think there’s a whole range of views on safety of AI systems and so on. You know, I’m sort of of the view that those are a little overblown. I think like careful engineering of what we allow AI systems to do will enable us to have safe deployment of these systems even though they are quite capable.

You know, I think misinformation is one that I’m worried about in the nearer term, because that seems like now we can create incredibly realistic video and audio things that are hard to distinguish even for super sophisticated people and with a lot of time to look at them. So that seems like one area that I think will be a worry.

And I think also just how do we manage the impact of AI being able to do things that previously it wasn’t able to do, and how do we make sure that people are prepared for those transitions and can learn to use these new tools and can be more productive and more effective using these tools, than what could happen, which is all of a sudden people suddenly can’t do that because it’s been.

Hallucinations at the limits of a long context

Joey: I’m Joey. I’m a senior in computer science. I had a question about hallucinations and specifically like long behavior, especially as we’re getting more workflows and like longer contexts. We know that like even though past models claim to have one million context window, at the limits of that 1 million context window the retention and like quality of responses, beyond simply adding search into the language model, what are other ways that Gemini has been prioritizing decreasing especially more like critical applications like.

Jeff Dean: Yeah, I mean I would say one of the key techniques is instead of just generating a single answer, having multiple rollouts of potential answers and then having the model itself look at those rollouts and assess which one it thinks is most, or which pieces of them it thinks are most likely correct.

That essentially is using much more inference time compute, or chain of thought style thinking. Those kinds of things can definitely decrease the rate of hallucinations. I mean that’s sort of the kind of approach we use in some of the IMO work, where you really can’t afford to hallucinate because you need to prove this problem, one of these six problems, correct.

And so that has been quite a good tool to rely on. But that also brings back the question of inference efficiency, because you’d really like for every answer to produce 16 answers and look at them and decide which ones you want to throw out and which ones you want to keep.

LLMs against the emerging world models

Audience member: I’m curious what’s your point of view of LLMs versus the emerging world models that are coming up or being worked on from a research.

Jeff Dean: Yeah, I mean I think world models are really just do you understand multiple modalities and how the world works from a physics perspective and so on. You know, I think a lot of our Gemini models are actually pretty good at doing world models.

You know, if you look at the Genie 3 releases, those are built on top of Gemini models and enable you to generate fairly sophisticated imaginary worlds with text prompts and then control interaction in that world. So you can move left, move right, jump, move forward and move back. And it maintains consistency with the world that it has created. And if you turn left and then turn back right, the things that were there are still there. So that’s an important thing.

Note

Editor’s note. DeepMind’s Genie 3 announcement presents it as the third model in the Genie line of world models, after Genie 1 and Genie 2, and does not describe it as built on Gemini. The relationship Dean states here is not part of the public material.

You know, we’re actually collaborating with our Waymo colleagues, because that enables them to create long-tail training cases in simulation. So you can say, please make a scenario where an elephant appears in the middle of the road, and that enables you to create dozens and dozens of test cases that are really hard to actually have occur in the real world. And you can see how the car behaves. And it actually even synthesizes the LiDAR data that the system would have, enabling you to get better safety properties.

What to research with a thousand TPUs

Host: Maybe one more question, Jeff, you can. [laughter]

Audience member: All right, not high not low but middle. Hi. I guess like the last question, research. I’m kind of curious what type of research you think we should work on about a thousand TPUs, because a few of the directions we talked about are like pretty data intensive.

Jeff Dean: Yeah.

Audience member: What do you think we can do to help the AI forward?

Jeff Dean: Yeah. I mean, I think a lot of the kinds of work we do from a research perspective start as investigations at very small scale, right? And so I think where you can be quite effective is trying lots of different things that maybe you’re not training on a thousand accelerators, but you’re demonstrating at small scale this idea has legs. Right? Like there’s all kinds of problems in say continual learning or different model architectures.

And in particular one of the things we do is we run extremely extremely small, extremely small, and small. And we look at the trend of those things, because that trend is often more indicative of importance than exactly where it falls relative to the current baseline state-of-the-art of our extra extra small or extra small or small model.

Right? If the slope, if it’s below the baseline, but the slope looks good, that’s a really interesting idea. If it’s above the baseline at the absolute smallest scale but rapidly plummeting below the baseline even at the small scale, that’s less interesting.

And so I think where people who don’t have access to large scale compute can really do a great job is focusing on solutions that are quite different and quite interesting and not stress about getting state-of-the-art results. And I think we as a community also should say this is very different and unique and doesn’t achieve state-of-the-art results but it looks interesting at small scale. Like we should, as conference reviewers or whatever, celebrate that kind of thing than something that gets an incremental improvement on state-of-the-art by tweaking one little thing that is actually not that interesting. Question. Okay. [applause]

item.title: Young Adults in the U.S. Are Increasingly Wary of AI
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

Colleen McClain and Eugenie Park at Pew Research Center report that American concern about AI is still rising, and that adults under 30 are the group whose concern has kept climbing instead of levelling off after 2023. The survey covered 3,488 U.S. adults from June 22 to 28, 2026, through the Center’s American Trends Panel, with the questionnaire, topline, and methodology published alongside it.

What the survey finds:

  • Most Americans lean concerned. 52% say the increased use of AI in daily life makes them more concerned than excited, up from 37% in 2021. 9% are more excited than concerned, and 37% feel both equally.

  • Under-30s cross a majority for the first time. 55% of adults aged 18 to 29 are more concerned than excited, up from 31% in 2021 and 47% a year ago. Their excitement fell from 25% to 11% over the same period.

  • The older groups rose earlier, by 2023. Their 2026 readings are 51% for ages 30 to 49, 47% for 50 to 64, and 59% for 65 and older, against 48%, 59%, and 61% in 2023.

  • Expected job losses are up seven points. 71% think AI will lead to fewer jobs in the U.S. over the next 20 years, against 64% in 2024. 5% expect more jobs, 10% expect no real difference, and 14% are unsure.

  • Young adults now match ages 30 to 64. 73% of under-30s expect fewer jobs, up from 61% in 2024. They are now level with ages 30 to 49 (74%) and 50 to 64 (72%). Adults 65 and older are lowest at 63%.

Pew also cites its earlier work on the same age group. Adults under 30 are the group most likely to say AI will be bad for society and bad for them personally, and to expect it to make connection and creativity harder to come by. Most of them use chatbots, and they are about as likely to say the tools hurt their own creativity as help it.

My Notes

  • Expectations moved most where employment actually fell. Under-30s’ expectation of fewer jobs rose 12 points since 2024, ahead of 8 points for ages 30 to 49 and 3 points for 50 to 64. The payroll data is ordered the same way. The AI Entry-Level Jobs Effect Isn’t Fading put employment for workers aged 22 to 25 in the most AI-exposed occupations down about 3.8% a year, ages 31 to 34 down 1.7%, and ages 35 to 40 growing at 2%. AI and Job Postings: From Destruction to Creation? found the software-posting rebound going to senior roles. Adults 65 and older rose 5 points, and the payroll data does not cover them.

  • Concern is falling among 50-to-64-year-olds. Concern among adults aged 50 to 64 peaked at 59% in 2023 and has come down every year since, to 47% in 2026. They are now the least concerned of the four age groups, and the only one whose concern is falling. Their excitement stayed flat at 7% to 8% across those years. Pew does not say why.

    • Only the three-year fall clears sampling error. Pew’s methodology puts 902 respondents in this age band, at a margin of error of plus or minus 3.5 points. The 12-point drop since 2023 is well outside that. The three single-year steps of 3, 4, and 5 points each fall inside it, so “falling every year” describes the point estimates rather than three separate declines.
    • Their expectation of job loss barely moved. Their 3-point rise since 2024 is the smallest of any working-age group, and it fits the payroll data. The series in The AI Entry-Level Jobs Effect Isn’t Fading comes from the Stanford Digital Economy Lab and ADP Canaries Dashboard. The dashboard has employment growing about 2% a year for workers aged 35 to 40 while the 22-to-25 cohort contracts about 3.8%. The dashboard’s age bands stop short of 50 to 64, so that is the direction of the gradient and not a reading for this group.
    • Direct experience may be lowering their concern. Chatbot use in this group rose from 25% to 42% between 2024 and 2026, per Pew’s February 2026 age report. On that survey’s separate positive-or-negative question they gave AI’s effect on society the highest positive rating of any age group, 18%. The conjecture has a clear counterexample: under-30s use chatbots most of all, 66%, and are the most concerned, so exposure by itself does not lower concern.

Related Posts

  • The AI Entry-Level Jobs Effect Isn’t Fading: the payroll series that gives under-30s a concrete reason for the job-loss expectation.
  • AI and Job Postings: From Destruction to Creation?: postings data showing the recovery going to senior rather than early-career roles.
  • Daron Acemoglu on AI, Jobs, and Liberal Democracy: the argument that a labor market which stops delivering shared prosperity becomes a political problem.
  • Who Will Actually Thrive in the Hybrid AI-Human Work Force?: the counterweight, asking which workers benefit from the same deployment.
  • GPTs Are GPTs: Labor Market Impact of Large Language Models: the early occupation-exposure estimate these public expectations can be measured against.

item.title: CRAG — Comprehensive RAG Benchmark
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

In CRAG — Comprehensive RAG Benchmark [1] (NeurIPS 2024 Datasets and Benchmarks Track), Xiao Yang, Kai Sun, Hao Xin, and Yushi Sun (equal contribution), with Xin Luna Dong as last author and 22 co-authors from Meta and HKUST, release 4,409 factual questions paired with a frozen retrieval world: up to 50 full web pages per question, a mock knowledge graph of 2.6 million entities, and 38 mock APIs. Retrieval-augmented generation is scored on a metric that subtracts hallucinations from correct answers, and on that metric no straightforward RAG configuration beats prompting GPT-4 Turbo with no retrieval at all.

Four constructions the post uses throughout:

  • The four answer labels and the truthfulness score: a response is perfect (correct, nothing hallucinated), acceptable (useful, minor errors), missing (“I don’t know,” an error, or a request to clarify), or incorrect. The four labels score , , , and , and truthfulness is the mean over the evaluation set. The automatic evaluation uses only accurate, incorrect, and missing, so every truthfulness figure in Table 5 is exactly accuracy minus hallucination, to within rounding. The negative weight on incorrect is the design decision that makes CRAG’s primary metric behave differently from accuracy: a system can raise its accuracy and lower its truthfulness in the same step.
  • The three tasks, each nesting inside the next. Task 1 supplies five web pages per question and tests answer generation alone. Task 2 adds the mock APIs over the mock knowledge graph, testing whether a system can query structured data and merge it with text. Task 3 supplies 50 web pages instead of five plus the APIs, which adds ranking to the test, since more pages hold both more answers and more noise.
  • Dynamism: how fast the answer to a question changes. The four buckets are real-time, fast-changing, slow-changing, and static, and they are distributed 10%, 13%, 23%, and 54% across the benchmark. Finance is 42% real-time, and Movie is 76% static.
  • Popularity: whether a question’s entity is head, torso, or tail, sampled from the knowledge graph following the Head-to-Tail method [2] by four of the same authors. The 1,984 knowledge-graph questions split almost evenly, 661 head, 658 torso, 665 tail, so the popularity slices are the same size by construction rather than by accident.

Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has recently emerged as a promising solution to alleviate Large Language Model (LLM)’s deficiency in lack of knowledge. Existing RAG datasets, however, do not adequately represent the diverse and dynamic nature of real-world Question Answering (QA) tasks. To bridge this gap, we introduce the Comprehensive RAG Benchmark (CRAG), a factual question answering benchmark of 4,409 question-answer pairs and mock APIs to simulate web and Knowledge Graph (KG) search. CRAG is designed to encapsulate a diverse array of questions across five domains and eight question categories, reflecting varied entity popularity from popular to long-tail, and temporal dynamisms ranging from years to seconds. Our evaluation of this benchmark highlights the gap to fully trustworthy QA. Whereas most advanced LLMs achieve accuracy on CRAG, adding RAG in a straightforward manner improves the accuracy only to 44%. State-of-the-art industry RAG solutions only answer 63% of questions without any hallucination. CRAG also reveals much lower accuracy in answering questions regarding facts with higher dynamism, lower popularity, or higher complexity, suggesting future research directions. The CRAG benchmark laid the groundwork for a KDD Cup 2024 challenge and attracted thousands of participants and submissions. We commit to maintaining CRAG to serve research communities in advancing RAG solutions and general QA solutions. CRAG is available at https://github.com/facebookresearch/CRAG/.

Methods

The questions come from two sources. Knowledge-graph questions start from 600-plus hand-written templates over selected entity types and relations, filled by sampling head, torso, and tail entities; that produces 1,984 questions. Web questions start from annotators writing what a user might plausibly ask (“most popular action movies in 2023”) and building the answer from the search results; that produces 2,425. Every ground truth is checked by hand. Both halves span five domains — Finance, Sports, Music, Movie, and Open — and eight question types.

The eight CRAG question types. Table 2 from the paper [1], condensed.
Question type What it asks for
Simple a fact unlikely to change, such as a birth date or a book’s authors
Simple with condition a simple fact under a constraint, such as a stock price on a given date
Set a set of entities, such as the continents in the southern hemisphere
Comparison a comparison between two entities, such as who started performing earlier
Aggregation a count or total over retrieved results, such as how many Oscars an actor won
Multi-hop a chain across several facts, such as who acted in a director’s latest film
Post-processing-heavy reasoning over the retrieved facts, such as how many days someone served
False premise a question resting on something untrue, such as naming an album that does not exist

Simple and simple-with-condition together are 43% of the benchmark, so the six complex types share the remaining 57% and each is sized to be measurable on its own. The paper states that most slices are large enough for a margin of error under 5% at 95% confidence.

The retrieval side is what separates CRAG from a question list. For each question, the question text went to the Brave Search API and up to 50 full HTML pages were stored, 220,000 pages in total. The release also includes mock knowledge graphs holding the public data the questions were generated from, plus randomly chosen same-type entities and deliberate hard negatives with confusable names, “phantom” as a distractor for “phantom of the opera.” Thirty-eight mock APIs expose that graph through calls with named parameters, get_price_history(ticker) and the like. Web and knowledge-graph snapshots were taken at the same moment the real-time questions were posed, so the whole retrieval world is one consistent frozen instant.

CRAG against existing factual-QA benchmarks. Table 1 from the paper [1].
Benchmark Web KG Mock API Dynamic Torso/tail Beyond Wikipedia Questions
QALD-10 ✗ ✓ ✗ ✗ ✗ ✗ 0.8K
MS MARCO ✓ ✗ ✗ not explicitly not explicitly ✓ 100K
Natural Questions ✓ ✗ ✗ not explicitly not explicitly ✗ 323K
RGB [3] ✓ ✗ ✗ ✗ ✗ ✓ 1K
FreshLLMs [4] ✗ ✗ ✗ ✓ ✗ ✓ 0.6K
CRAG ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ 4.4K

CRAG is two orders of magnitude smaller than Natural Questions and MS MARCO, and the argument for it is the column count rather than the row count. It is the only entry that combines web retrieval, knowledge-graph search, mock APIs, questions whose answers move, deliberate coverage of unpopular entities, and sources outside Wikipedia.

Figure 2 measures whether the frozen corpus can answer its own questions, by asking Llama 3 70B Instruct whether the retrieved pages contain enough to answer, given the question and the ground truth. Two curves: page snippets alone reach 64.4% recall at 50 pages, and full page content reaches 84.6%, a gap of about 20 points that is the case for parsing HTML rather than stopping at the search-result summary. Both curves are steep and then flat, with the top five pages already at 69.4%. That the ceiling is 85% rather than 100% is deliberate: a system that cannot answer the remaining 15% should say so, which is what the missing label and the zero score exist to reward.

Scoring uses both human grading and a two-step automatic evaluation. If the answer matches the ground truth exactly it counts as accurate. Otherwise two evaluator models, gpt-3.5-turbo-0125 and llama-3-70B-instruct, judge it accurate, incorrect, or missing, and the reported numbers average the two. Using two evaluators from different families is a guard against a model preferring its own output. Against human grading the automatic method reaches F1 of 94.7% with ChatGPT and 98.9% with Llama 3. The data splits 30% validation, 30% public test, 40% private, with the private split reserved for the KDD Cup leaderboard.

Results

The first experiment runs on the 1,335-question public test set. Prompts encourage brief answers and explicitly invite “I don’t know” when confidence is low, which matters given that a missing answer scores zero and an incorrect one scores . Eight models were tried, and the paper reports the two strongest, Llama 3 70B Instruct and GPT-4 Turbo. Context windows are fixed per model rather than per task, 4K tokens of web text and 2K of knowledge-graph results for these two, filled by concatenating page snippets in their original order. Entity extraction for the API calls uses llama-3-8B-instruct with in-context examples.

The findings:

  • Accuracy climbs with each task (Table 5). GPT-4 Turbo goes 33.5% with no retrieval, 35.9% on Task 1, 41.3% on Task 2, 43.6% on Task 3. Llama 3 70B Instruct climbs the same way, from 32.3% to 40.6%. Each step adds a few points: web pages, then structured data, then ranking over a larger candidate set.
  • Truthfulness does not follow accuracy (Table 5, last column). GPT-4 Turbo scores 20.0 with no retrieval and 7.7, 16.2, and 13.4 across the three RAG tasks, so every retrieval configuration is worse than none. Llama 3 70B Instruct moves the other way, 3.4 to 4.5 to 8.3 to 9.1. The mechanism is visible one column left: GPT-4 Turbo’s hallucination rate more than doubles from 13.5% to 28.2% on Task 1, because retrieval converts answers it would have declined to give into answers grounded in the wrong passage.
  • GPT-4 Turbo’s missing rate falls from 53% to 36% (Table 5, Missing column). Unaided, GPT-4 Turbo declines to answer 53.0% of questions. With five web pages it declines only 35.9% of the time, and roughly all of the recovered volume lands in the hallucination column rather than the accuracy column.
  • Structured data is the only step that improves both numbers (Table 5, Task 1 against Task 2). Adding the mock APIs takes GPT-4 Turbo from 35.9% to 41.3% accuracy while cutting hallucination from 28.2% to 25.1%, which the paper attributes to knowledge-graph facts being brief and precise.
  • Ranking loses over 30% of the retrieved answers (§5.1). Over 30% of questions have their ground truth in the retrieved web pages but outside the context window, which is why Task 3’s 50 pages beat Task 2’s five despite bringing more noise with them.
  • Retrieval helps unpopular entities and hurts popular ones (§5.1 and Figure 3(c)). GPT-4 Turbo’s unaided truthfulness falls from 21% on head entities to 11% on torso to 8% on tail. Adding retrieval lifts torso by 7 points and tail by 6 but lowers head by 4. For well-known entities the model’s stored knowledge is better than what retrieval brings it.

Figure 3 breaks the same two models into four panels, unaided against full Task 3 retrieval. Negative bars are systems that hallucinate more than they answer correctly, and there are many of them. Panel (b) is the clearest: at real-time dynamism, Llama 3 70B Instruct goes from unaided to with retrieval, and GPT-4 Turbo from to . Panel (d) holds the largest single move anywhere in the figure. On false premise questions, GPT-4 Turbo goes from unaided to with web and knowledge-graph context, a 60-point collapse. Panels (a) and (c) show the two directions coexisting: retrieval is worth 20 to 30 points on Music, Movie, and Open domain questions, and worth less than nothing on Finance and Sports.

The second experiment queried five deployed systems with the same questions and graded the answers by hand:

  • Copilot Pro leads the five deployed systems (Table 6). Copilot Pro reaches 50.6 truthfulness with 62.6% perfect answers, then Gemini Advanced at 49.3, ChatGPT Plus at 41.5, Meta SG at 41.4, and Perplexity.ai at 34.9. The paper notes these are not strictly comparable to Table 5, which used automatic rather than human grading and different retrieval access.
  • Hallucination stays between 16% and 25% for all five (Table 6, Hall. column). No deployed system has solved the problem that makes truthfulness diverge from accuracy. The best is Meta SG at 16.0% and the worst Perplexity.ai at 25.3%.
  • The most truthful system is also the slowest (Table 6, Latency column). Copilot Pro takes 11.6 seconds per answer, Meta SG 3.4 seconds with mid-table truthfulness, so the five systems occupy visibly different points on the same trade-off.
  • Three of the five score negative on real-time questions (cover figure, panel b). Gemini Advanced scores , Perplexity.ai , and ChatGPT Plus , against Copilot Pro at and Meta SG at . Fast-changing questions are better but still thin, from to .
  • Set and false-premise questions flip from negative to positive (cover figure, panel d). Both types were badly negative for straightforward RAG and are comfortably positive for every deployed system, set answers from 55 to 68 and false premises from 36 to 72. Whatever the deployed systems do about premises and completeness is not in the straightforward baseline.

My Notes

  • RAGuard found the same pattern eight months later: no straightforward RAG configuration here passes the 20% truthfulness that GPT-4 Turbo reaches unaided (§5.1). RAGuard [5] reported in February 2025 that every one of eight models scored below its own no-retrieval baseline on political fact-checking, and that the strongest zero-context model lost the most. The two use different corpora and different domains.
  • Only the structured source improved both scores: Task 2 is the only step in Table 5 where accuracy rises and hallucination falls together, and that holds for both models. OKGQA [6] (ACL 2025) put the two retrieval sources side by side on open-ended questions: knowledge-graph triplets took GPT-4o’s FActScore from 55.4% with no external knowledge to 72.6%, and the graph-based methods beat IRCoT, a Wikipedia-paragraph baseline, on correctness and on both factuality metrics, SAFE and FActScore, which the authors attribute to the irrelevant and conflicting passages that come with retrieved text. The same paper’s perturbed-graph variant is the caveat: the advantage narrows as the graph degrades, so it depends on how clean the graph is.
  • Retrieval hurts false-premise questions most: a question about an album that does not exist still retrieves plenty of true material about the artist, and topically on-target material looks like corroboration of a premise it never addresses. That is the likely mechanism behind Figure 3(d)’s 60-point collapse. AbstentionBench [7] treats false premises as one of five categories where a model should decline, and finds reasoning fine-tuning degrades that behaviour. CRAG points at a second way to lose it, and the paper does not say how the deployed systems avoid it.
  • Deployed systems lose their edge on images: the paper promised multi-modal and multi-turn extensions, and CRAG-MM [8] delivered them in October 2025 and hosted KDD Cup 2025. On its single-turn questions straightforward RAG reaches 32% truthfulness and deployed industry systems also reach 32%, so the gap Table 6 shows here is gone in the new modality.

item.title: LiveFact: A Dynamic, Time-Aware Benchmark for LLM-Driven Fake News Detection
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

In LiveFact: A Dynamic, Time-Aware Benchmark for LLM-Driven Fake News Detection [1] (ACL 2026, pages 11881–11910), Cheng Xu, Changhong Jin, Yingjie Niu, Nan Yan, Yuke Mei, Shuhao Guan, Liming Chen, and M-Tahar Kechadi (University College Dublin, Georgia Tech, Dalian University of Technology, and Bebxy) build a fake-news benchmark that is rebuilt monthly from fresh news events. Each model gets only the evidence that existed a chosen number of days before or after the event it is asked about, so the question becomes whether the model says “ambiguous” when the evidence to decide does not exist yet.

Figure 1 above is the paper’s cost-performance summary of the November 2025 release. It puts each model’s average score across the benchmark against the dollar cost of one full evaluation run, with marker size for parameter count and color for family: Qwen in blue, Llama in green, DeepSeek in purple, and OpenAI’s GPT models as grey diamonds. The shaded band in the upper left is the cheap-and-accurate corner, and the starred point inside it is Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507, which scores within three points of the best model in the set for about a fourteenth of what gpt-5.2 costs to evaluate.

Four constructions the post relies on:

  • Benchmark data contamination (BDC): the benchmark’s test items have been absorbed into a model’s pretraining corpus, so a high score can come from recall instead of reasoning. Every static benchmark accumulates this exposure as models are retrained, which is the problem a monthly rebuild is meant to avoid.
  • Time-sliced evidence set : for an event with headline date , the evidence published no later than , with days. is the state of public knowledge three days before the event, three days after. The paper calls the condition the “fog of war.”
  • Dual-mode evaluation: the same prediction is scored against two different ground truths. In Classification Mode the target is the claim’s eventual factual status, which does not change with . In Inference Mode the target is what a human expert could justifiably conclude from alone, so a claim that turns out to be Real is labeled Ambiguous at if the confirming evidence had not appeared yet. Both modes draw from the same three labels, Real, Fake, and Ambiguous.
  • SSA Factor: the contamination indicator, , borrowed from the Semantic Sensitivity Amplifier (SSA) framework the same group published at EMNLP 2025 [2]. is the score drop from swapping real named entities for invented ones and (Overturn Rate) is the share of items whose predicted label changes under that swap. A model whose answers move when only the names move is keying on memorized entities.

The rapid development of Large Language Models (LLMs) has transformed fake news detection and fact-checking tasks from simple classification to complex reasoning. However, evaluation frameworks have not kept pace. Current benchmarks are static, making them vulnerable to benchmark data contamination (BDC) and ineffective at assessing reasoning under temporal uncertainty. To address this, we introduce LiveFact a continuously updated benchmark that simulates the real-world “fog of war” in misinformation detection. LiveFact uses dynamic, temporal evidence sets to evaluate models on their ability to reason with evolving, incomplete information rather than on memorized knowledge. We propose a dual-mode evaluation: Classification Mode for final verification and Inference Mode for evidence-based reasoning, along with a component to monitor BDC explicitly. Tests with 22 LLMs show that open-source Mixture-of-Experts models, such as Qwen3-235B-A22B, now match or outperform proprietary state-of-the-art systems. More importantly, our analysis finds a significant “reasoning gap.” Capable models exhibit epistemic humility by recognizing unverifiable claims in early data slices-an aspect traditional static benchmarks overlook. LiveFact sets a sustainable standard for evaluating robust, temporally aware AI verification.

Methods

The benchmark is a pipeline that runs on a monthly cycle rather than a dataset that was collected once. Five stages:

  • Event retrieval: the Google News API is scraped daily at 00:00 GMT for trending items in the World section, then deduplicated and filtered for overlapping storylines and low-relevance items. The November 2025 cycle yielded 737 distinct events.
  • Time-aware evidence construction: for each event, Google APIs are queried with hard timestamp bounds at , , and , producing the three evidence sets , , and . Across the 737 events this gathered 25,064 distinct pieces of evidence. To stay inside fair use, only page titles, source names, and publication timestamps are retained, with no article bodies stored or redistributed.
  • Claim and context generation: OpenAI’s o4-mini reads the headline and all time-stamped evidence for an event and writes a background Context describing the entities involved, plus a set of claims labeled Real, Fake, or Ambiguous. November 2025 produced 4,392 claims, initially 1,468 Real, 1,451 Fake, and 1,473 Ambiguous.
  • Human-in-the-loop verification: annotators check every generated claim against the retrieved evidence and correct inconsistencies. They also set the Inference Mode labels, deciding per time slice whether the available evidence is enough for a human expert to reach the correct verdict.
  • BDC risk monitoring: Qwen3-235B-A22B performs the entity swap, chosen over an OpenAI model to avoid preference leakage into a benchmark whose claims an OpenAI model wrote. The result is a parallel shifted dataset from which , the Overturn Rate, and the SSA Factor are computed each cycle.

Figure 2 lays out the three parts side by side:

  • Panel A is the monthly pipeline above, with the arrow from Stage 5 back into Stage 4 marking the point where the shifted dataset re-enters human review.
  • Panel B is the prediction the benchmark asks for, : the model under test, , reads the claim , one time-sliced evidence set , and the static background context , then emits a verdict for that slice. The timeline across the top makes the three evidence sets different objects rather than three samples of one.
  • Panel C splits the scoring. The same verdict is compared against a time-invariant target on the left and a time-dependent one on the right, and below that the entity-shift step turns the difference between original and shifted predictions into the SSA Factor.
Inference Mode label distribution across the three time slices, November 2025. Table 2 from the paper [1].
Evidence set Real Fake Ambiguous Total
346 348 3,698 4,392
1,404 1,390 1,598 4,392
1,460 1,443 1,489 4,392

The claim set is fixed at 4,392 items, and only the Inference Mode target moves. Three days before an event, human reviewers judged 3,698 of the 4,392 claims, 84% of them, unresolvable from the evidence then available. By the headline date it falls to 1,598, and three days after to 1,489. The paper is explicit that this makes accuracy unreliable at , since always answering Ambiguous scores 84% there, which is why macro-F1 is reported alongside it throughout.

Results

The evaluation setup behind Table 3:

  • Models: eighteen are evaluated on the November 2025 release, fourteen open-weights across the Qwen3, Llama 3, DeepSeek, Kimi, and GPT-OSS families and four proprietary OpenAI models, spanning 1B to 1T parameters. Table 5’s registry lists twenty-two, the extra four appearing only in the appendix training-mode ablation and extended-token runs. Six of the twenty-two are base checkpoints without instruction tuning, three of them among the eighteen scored in Table 3, and Table 5 classes two more of the eighteen, Qwen3-32B and Qwen3-8B, as hybrid rather than instruction-tuned.
  • Metrics: twelve per model, from accuracy and macro-F1 crossed with the two evaluation modes and the three time slices. The reported Avg. is the mean of all twelve.
  • Decoding: every model answers under the same protocol, temperature 0, top-p 1.0, and a 128-token generation cap the paper sets to keep verdicts concise, since scoring reads only a [[LABEL]] token out of whatever the model produces.
  • Star rows: reasoning-trained models spend that budget deliberating and get cut off before the label appears, so they were re-run at 1,024 tokens.

The findings:

  • The top of the leaderboard is open-weights (Table 3, Avg. column). Qwen3-235B-A22B-Instruct-2507 averages 72.40, gpt-oss-120b 72.13, gpt-5.1 72.02, and gpt-5.2 71.52. DeepSeek-V3.1 reaches 61.48 with 671B total parameters, below Qwen3-32B, a 32B dense model, at 66.03.
  • A 30B mixture-of-experts model gets within three points at a fourteenth of the cost (Figure 1). Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 averages 69.46 for $0.64 per run against $9.27 for gpt-5.2 (Table 6), and it is the only model inside the shaded region of the cover figure.
  • Base checkpoints answer Real to almost everything (Table 3, dagger rows). Llama-3.1-70B, Llama-3.2-3B, and Llama-3.2-1B all average near 22, with macro-F1 near 16.7 in Classification Mode across every slice, which is what a single-class prediction produces on a three-class problem. Their confusion matrices in the appendix put nearly all the mass in the Real column at every slice and in both modes. The paper attributes the base-model failure to non-compliance with the required [[LABEL]] output format, an explanation it documents for Llama-3.1-8B, which averages 5.14% in the appendix training-mode ablation and is not one of the eighteen in Table 3.
  • Reasoning models need a larger output budget (Table 3, star rows). At the 128-token cap Kimi-K2-Thinking averaged 1.76 and the two GPT-OSS models averaged about 26, against 54.60, 72.13, and 57.05 at 1,024 tokens (Table 12). The paper inspected the outputs and found deliberation cut off mid-stream rather than wrong verdicts.
  • Scores rise sharply once the event happens, then flatten (Figure 3, panel a). In Classification Mode the Qwen and GPT families climb from the low 50s at to the high 70s at , and gain roughly one further point by . Almost all the measured difficulty is in the pre-event slice.
  • Inference Mode recovers most of that drop for some models and not others (Figure 3, panel b). Where Classification Mode punishes a model for not knowing what had not happened, Inference Mode credits it for saying so, and DeepSeek moves opposite to the rest: highest of the four families at and lowest at .
  • The reasoning gap spans 65 points across the eighteen models (Figure 4). Taking Inference accuracy minus Classification accuracy at , Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct gains 38.0 points and Qwen3-32B 37.6, while Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct loses 21.2 and the three base checkpoints lose 25 to 27. The paper attributes the positive end to recognizing an information void, the negative end among instruction-tuned models to overconfidence, and the negative end among base models to format non-compliance.

My Notes

  • The Avg. column supports match and nothing more
    • The abstract claims open-weights mixture-of-experts models “now match or outperform proprietary state-of-the-art systems.” Match it supports comfortably. The ordering it does not.
    • The top three Avg. values span 0.38 points in total, and each is a single run with no confidence interval or repeated seed anywhere in the paper. The binomial standard error on one accuracy near 72% over 4,392 items is about 0.7 points, so the gaps between them are smaller than the noise on any one of the twelve numbers being averaged. The three were not measured under the same conditions either: gpt-oss-120b needed 1,024 output tokens to reach 72.13, where Qwen3-235B-A22B-Instruct-2507 reached 72.40 at 128.
    • Nor does open versus proprietary divide the top of the table by lab. gpt-oss-120b, second at 72.13, is OpenAI’s own open-weights release, and gpt-5.1, third at 72.02, is OpenAI’s proprietary one, 0.11 points apart. The match claim holds, but a reader who takes it as open ecosystems catching up to the labs would be reading these rows wrongly, since one lab supplied both sides of that comparison.
    • The gap between open and closed weights has been closing on aggregate indices for a while, and a 0.38-point ordering on one benchmark adds little to what those trend lines already show.
  • The reasoning gap is computed from the wrong metric

    • §3.4 argues that accuracy is misleading at because Ambiguous is 84% of the labels there, and that macro-F1 is the metric that “treats all classes equally.” Figure 4 then computes the reasoning gap from accuracy at exactly that slice. Recomputed from Table 3’s macro-F1 columns, for all eighteen models, in the accuracy order Figure 4 uses:
