    • The order barely moves. Fifteen of the eighteen gaps shrink toward zero, most by half or more, because accuracy at credits a model for agreeing with a label that covers 84% of the items and macro-F1 does not.

    • Two gaps flip from positive to negative. Kimi-K2-Thinking goes from to and gpt-oss-120b from to , so both cross out of the group the paper calls uncertainty aware. Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 shrinks from to , no longer distinguishable from zero, and gpt-oss-20b is the one model whose negative gap widens, from to .

  • The gap mostly measures how often a model says Ambiguous
    • Whichever metric it uses, the gap is scored at only, so it rewards a model for saying Ambiguous before the event and nothing in it tests whether the model gives a definite verdict once the evidence exists. The appendix confusion matrices allow that check, at , over the 1,390 claims whose Inference target is Fake.
    • gpt-5.2 and Qwen3-32B come out with nearly the same macro-F1 gap, and . At , gpt-5.2 answers Ambiguous on 11% of the Fake claims and Qwen3-32B on 62%. The first declines before the evidence exists and gives verdicts once it does. The second declines throughout. The gap scores them the same.
    • The rate runs from 0% for Llama-3.1-70B to 62% for Qwen3-32B, and it ranks all eighteen models close to the way the gap ranks them: Spearman against the accuracy gap and against the macro-F1 gap, or and with the three always-Real base checkpoints dropped. A model’s gap is largely a restatement of how readily it declines to answer.
    • Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct shows the same conflation from the other side, and it is why the gap does not order models by quality. It holds the largest gap on both metrics while answering Ambiguous on only 19% of the Fake claims, because at it labels 76% of the genuinely Ambiguous claims Real instead. It also has the lowest average of any instruction-tuned model at 49.96, while the best overall model is eighth on both gap orderings. AbstentionBench [3] reported the same across twenty datasets, that “scaling models is of little use” for abstention. Nothing in either ordering supports the abstract’s “capable models exhibit epistemic humility.”
    • Scoring a confidence estimate by calibration error alone fails the same way, since a model that answers “0.5” to everything is perfectly calibrated and useless.
  • A monthly rebuild needs monthly expert review
    • The paper’s own Limitations section names the binding constraint, expert review to separate Ambiguous from Fake in Inference Mode. The public record shows what that costs.
    • Four monthly slices are on Hugging Face, November 2025 through February 2026, with nothing since. The leaderboard site shows scored results for the first two of them, and its repository was last pushed at the end of July 2026.
    • A benchmark that stops refreshing becomes the static benchmark whose contamination risk was the reason to build it. The SSA Factor would detect when that has happened, and it is computed per release cycle, so it stops reporting at the same time the cycle does.

  • How Artificial Analysis Builds Its Intelligence Index: the other way to run a continuously refreshed leaderboard, and what it takes to keep one going once the paper describing it is published.

item.title: How AI Text Watermarking Works
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

Plain text lacks a clear spot for hidden signals. The characters themselves hold no extra data, and metadata disappears when you copy and paste. James Padolsey’s visual explainer shows where the mark goes instead: into which word the model picks when several would do equally well. The explanation is broken into five steps, each with an interactive figure that lets you roll dice. The piece accompanies declaude, a tool the author created to rewrite AI-generated text into plain prose.

The question stopped being theoretical this month. Google has marked text from the Gemini app since 2024 through SynthID, and Claude models released from August 2026 onward mark inside the model, worldwide, with older models to follow. Both companies are answering the same EU transparency rule, and they have read its scope differently.

The reaction was fast and unfriendly. Nobody argues that the mechanism fails to work. The arguments are about who ends up marked, what the marking costs the prose, and whether a rule that binds only the people who cannot evade it is worth having.

How the mark works

  • The model chooses between several valid options: When producing text, a model does not have one fixed next word. It works from a ranked list of candidates that have assigned probabilities. Often, two or three distinct words can each produce a correct sentence. A page of text contains hundreds of such cases. This flexibility provides capacity because the sentence stays functional no matter which candidate is chosen.

  • A secret key influences the selection: in the original method from Kirchenbauer et al. [1] (ICML 2023), a keyed hash splits the shortlist into a green half and a red half. Words placed in the green half get a slight boost in their probability. Two reasons keep this alteration concealed. The boost is modest enough that red words continue to be selected often. The green and red groups are also recomputed at each position using the words that appeared just before. Consequently, a particular word can be green in some contexts and red in others. Google’s SynthID-Text [2] (Nature 2024), the system now in use, swaps the probability bonus for a keyed elimination bracket applied to sampled candidates. It is calibrated so that the expected probability of a word, averaged over the key’s randomness, stays equal to the original model output. Scott Aaronson’s scheme, developed at OpenAI, produces the sampling randomness directly from the key.

  • Detection is arithmetic on the key: the system does not look at the prose itself. The detector recalculates the green or red label for each position and tallies the green tokens. When the text is unmarked or is evaluated with an incorrect key, the count remains close to fifty percent. A slight bias only reaches statistical significance after many positions. Therefore short passages are hard to classify. The teaching model described in the explainer needs 1,500 words to reach a green rate of about 55%.

  • Only unbroken stretches of the original phrasing count: a position’s color depends on the preceding words. That position supplies evidence only if a short window of the original phrasing is still present. Rewriting the text eliminates evidence at the change points while keeping the original sections unchanged. Typical paraphrasing lowers the signal but does not erase it. Kirchenbauer et al. [3] (ICLR 2024) reported that text heavily paraphrased by humans still activates a detector once 800 tokens are present, with a 1e-5 false-positive rate. Eliminating the mark demands a rewrite that contains no original phrasing. When evaluating open versions of the KGW and EXP schemes in MarkLLM [4] with the declaude full-rewrite method, roughly 0.5% of windows persist. Detection then falls from near certainty to random chance. The explainer models the residual evidence as , where denotes the surviving fraction, the document length, and the per-token strength.

What it means in practice

The explainer concludes with five consequences that often contradict common assumptions about watermarking:

  • Verification depends on the provider. Teachers, editors, and third-party detection sites cannot run the test. It needs a secret key or a service that the key-holder operates. Google presently provides an early-access SynthID detection portal, and Anthropic says its own tools are still under development.
  • Watermarking differs from AI detection. Products such as GPTZero try to determine authorship by analyzing writing styles. A watermark test is a particular statistical calculation that needs the private key.
  • A positive result shows handling instead of authorship. Anthropic documentation says that human-written text will be marked when Claude proofreads or translates it. A negative result offers little information since older models and extensive editing both yield clean scores for AI-generated content.
  • Short or restricted text holds almost no mark. Evidence accumulates with length, so a brief passage leaves a signal too weak to call. Where the next word is close to predictable, as in computer code, quotes, or fact lists, there is barely any room to encode information at all.
  • Only some designs withstand rewriting. Methods that assign colors to words according to their identity instead of their context are more resistant to paraphrasing. However, an attacker can eventually discover a fixed coloring scheme by gathering enough samples. For watermarks embedded in meaning rather than specific words, the explainer notes that the only known countermeasure is rewriting the text from an outline.

What the rule actually asks for

Article 50(2) of the EU AI Act requires providers of systems generating synthetic text to mark that output in a machine-readable format. The same provision then carves out an exception. The obligation “shall not apply to the extent the AI systems perform an assistive function for standard editing or do not substantially alter the input data provided by the deployer or the semantics thereof.” It binds providers, and it does not oblige every person who uses AI to announce it.

The accompanying Code of Practice on Transparency of AI-Generated Content is reported to add three conditions:

  • It applies only to text longer than 200 tokens, roughly 150 words.
  • Providers must forbid watermark removal in their terms of service.
  • The mark should survive ordinary handling such as screenshots, scanning, copy-and-paste, and translation.

Anthropic’s implementation is broader than the exception would require. Marking happens at the model level, worldwide, across every product, which means it also covers the assistive editing the provision sets aside. Its help-center article announced the change without describing the method. A second post published a day later gives the mechanism and confirms Claude uses “a version of the SynthID-Text approach.”

The objection

Two critiques landed within days, and they attack different things.

Padolsey’s companion post argues the law fails on its own terms, because it binds only people who cannot circumvent it. He expects that group to overlap with the people who most need the help, “disabled and neurodivergent individuals, or those in circumstances that afford them less time and capacity for the ordinary expenditure of cognitive effort involved in prose-writing.”

His analogy is the calculator. A sum from a brain and a sum from a calculator are treated alike, and spellcheckers raised no alarm. Singling out assistance “only once the tool becomes capable enough to compose a whole sentence is not a principled boundary. It is a moral premium placed on difficulty itself.” His verdict on the blanket implementation is that it produces “a signal broad enough to implicate harmless and assistive use, yet fragile enough to be removed by a motivated person through substantial recomposition.”

John Gruber attacks the technique itself. No two synonyms mean the same thing, so a keyed nudge between them is a change in meaning however small, and the trade-off buys the writer nothing in speed, cost, or quality. He calls Anthropic’s “imperceptible” and “doesn’t change the meaning, quality, or readability” language false. What bothers him most is the consequence for a reader: with a secret key steering the choices, “we have no idea whether it completed to ‘mango and bananas’ because bananas was determined to be the best next token, or because bananas is in the ‘green’ bucket of words. It calls every single word choice into question.”

Both providers answer with measurement. Anthropic reports no impact on content, creativity, or readability in internal testing. The Nature paper [2] ran the larger experiment, comparing roughly 20 million watermarked and unwatermarked Gemini responses: thumbs-up rates differed by 0.01% and thumbs-down rates by 0.02%, both statistically insignificant. Gruber’s reply is that the instrument cannot see the effect he is describing, since nobody downvotes a response over bananas instead of pineapple.

Whether a strong watermark is achievable at all is a separate question. Zhang and colleagues [5] give an impossibility result for strong watermarking of generative models, and Sadasivan and colleagues [6] show paraphrase attacks defeating a range of detectors. Work continues on marks that survive recomposition by keying on meaning rather than wording [7], which is the family the explainer says only outline-level regeneration defeats.

My Notes

  • Anthropic’s key cannot detect other companies’ text: people ask first whether this can keep machine text out of a corpus, whether that corpus is training data, a journal’s submission pile, or a marketplace’s listings. Anthropic rules that out. Its key answers exactly one question: “What is the likelihood this was partly written by Claude?” It also “can’t tell whether the text was written by a different AI (even if that other AI uses watermarking, it would have a different key).” Screening all AI text would take every provider’s key, or every provider’s checking service.

  • Exam answers are the hardest case to check: the documents that trigger AI-writing accusations are the ones the mark covers worst. A short essay answer, a paragraph pasted into a longer document, a code snippet, and a block of quoted facts all leave too little signal to call. A record-low in-person final at Brown is the kind of case people want a provenance signal for, and a timed exam answer is close to the worst case for one.

  • Only Anthropic’s marking covers the API: on Google’s own developer forum, a Google-titled responder told an EU game developer on August 5, 2026 that Gemini API text is not SynthID-watermarked. Native text watermarking, the responder added, “is not planned at the moment.” The explainer calls this a documented exception, though the documentation is a forum reply. Anthropic went the other way, reaching the API and the cloud resellers. So one obligation produced opposite answers on the interface developers actually build against: with Claude you can point at the provider’s marking, and with the Gemini API you implement Article 50(2) yourself.

  • The wash was measured on the weaker schemes: the Nature paper [2] reports SynthID-Text beating both KGW and EXP on detectability at equal text length. Those two are what the full-rewrite test ran against, and SynthID-Text is what both production systems use. So the erasure result comes from the baselines the deployed scheme was built to beat, and nobody outside the providers can repeat it on production output.

  • Nothing technical prevents a key per account: the mechanism does not require one key per provider. A key that varied by account would work the same way, and it would identify the customer behind a passage as well as the model. Anthropic addresses this. The watermark “carries no identifying information and can’t be traced to a specific person, organization, or chat,” and nothing in it or its key would let anyone recover information about a user or their chats. The scheme itself does not supply that guarantee. Anthropic’s configuration choice does.

References

The SynthID-Text paper. https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-024-08025-4
  3. Kirchenbauer, J., Geiping, J., Wen, Y., Shu, M., Saifullah, K., Kong, K., Fernando, K., Saha, A., Goldblum, M., Goldstein, T. “On the Reliability of Watermarks for Large Language Models.” ICLR 2024 (arXiv:2306.04634). https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.04634

item.title: QuanTemp: A Real-World Open-Domain Benchmark for Fact-Checking Numerical Claims
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

In QuanTemp: A real-world open-domain benchmark for fact-checking numerical claims [1] (SIGIR 2024, July 2024), Venktesh V (TU Delft), Abhijit Anand (L3S Research Center), Avishek Anand (TU Delft), and Vinay Setty (University of Stavanger and Factiverse) release 15,514 real numerical claims drawn from 45 fact-checking organizations, together with a 423,320-snippet web evidence corpus that excludes fact-checking sites, and report that the strongest of their baselines reaches 58.32 macro-F1. The claims, questions, and evidence corpus are released alongside the paper.

Four definitions first:

  • Numerical claim: a statement that needs verification of any explicit or implicit quantitative or temporal content. That is broader than “contains a number,” since it covers comparisons and date-relative statements where the quantity is implied rather than written out. It is also why the dataset ends up with a temporal category alongside a statistical one.
  • Claim decomposition: rewriting a claim into a set of sub-questions, then using those questions rather than the claim itself as search queries. The paper evaluates two published decomposers, and the choice of decomposer turns out to matter more than the choice of verdict model.
  • Unified evidence versus gold evidence: the two retrieval settings. Unified evidence means the system retrieves from the released corpus, which is the realistic setting. Gold evidence means the system is handed the fact-checker’s own justification paragraph, which is an upper bound on what any retriever could supply.
  • Macro-F1 (M-F1) versus weighted-F1 (W-F1): the label distribution is 57.93% False, 23.27% Conflicting, 18.79% True, so weighted-F1 tracks the False class and macro-F1 is the number that moves when a system gets better at the two minority classes. Both are reported throughout, and they disagree about how much progress there has been.

With the growth of misinformation on the web, automated fact checking has garnered immense interest for detecting growing misinformation and disinformation. Current systems have made significant advancements in handling synthetic claims sourced from Wikipedia, and noteworthy progress has been achieved in addressing real-world claims that are verified by fact-checking organizations as well. We compile and release QuanTemp, a diverse, multi-domain dataset focused exclusively on numerical claims, encompassing comparative, statistical, interval, and temporal aspects, with detailed metadata and an accompanying evidence collection. This addresses the challenge of verifying real-world numerical claims, which are complex and often lack precise information, a gap not filled by existing works that mainly focus on synthetic claims. We evaluate and quantify these gaps in existing solutions for the task of verifying numerical claims. We also evaluate claim decomposition based methods, numerical understanding based natural language inference (NLI) models and our best baselines achieves a macro-F1 of 58.32. This demonstrates that QuanTemp serves as a challenging evaluation set for numerical claim verification.

Methods

The cover figure traces the construction pipeline end to end, left to right. Fact-checking sites supply real-world claims, a quantity segmenter marks the numeric spans in each claim, and a filter keeps only the claims that pass the numerical test. Two claim-decomposition methods then turn each survivor into sub-questions, those questions go to Google, and the pooled results become the evidence corpus. Five stages, each of which discards or adds something specific:

  • Claim collection: the Google Fact Check Tools API returns 278,636 fact-checks as of 15 November 2023. Dropping non-English fact-checks leaves 139,926 from 45 organizations. Politifact contributes the largest share at 3,840 claims, then Snopes at 1,648. The top source countries are the USA (6,215), India (1,356), and the UK (596).
  • Quantity segmentation: the claim is parsed into a constituency tree, nodes tagged with the cardinal-number part of speech CD are located, and the noun phrases at their least common ancestors are extracted as quantitative segments. Requiring one segment admits false positives such as “the one and only,” so the filter requires more than one segment, excluding bare nouns like “Covid-19.” A self-assessment on 1,000 sampled claims puts the heuristic at 95% accuracy. This is the step that cuts 139,926 fact-checks down to 15,514 numerical claims.
  • Label standardization: source labels from 45 organizations are mapped onto True, False, and Conflicting following the AVeriTeC [2] convention, and claims with unclear or absent labels are dropped.
  • Claim decomposition: two published methods generate the search queries. ClaimDecomp [3] produces yes/no sub-questions, reproduced here by prompting gpt-3.5-turbo with in-context examples from the original ClaimDecomp training set. Program-FC [4] produces a program of Verify(...) calls instead, one call per aspect of the claim. A third condition uses the unmodified claim as the query.
  • Evidence collection: the claim and every generated question are submitted to Google through a commercial search API, the top 10 results per query are kept, results from over 150 fact-checking domains are filtered out, and the per-query result lists are merged by top- document pooling. What survives is 423,320 snippets. Wikipedia is the largest source at 28,124 snippets, followed by nytimes.com at 8,430 and ncbi.nlm.nih.gov at 8,417. The authors flag 2,889 snippets from youtube.com as a surprise, and on inspection those are news-video transcripts and descriptions.

Table 1 is where the paper places itself against the field, and the two rightmost columns are the argument. The upper block is synthetic claims written from Wikipedia or a knowledge base: FEVER [5] at 185,445 claims, FEVEROUS [6] at 87,026, TabFact at 92,283, all marked as lacking a numerical focus. The lower block is claims taken from fact-checking sites: LIAR at 12,836, MultiFC at 36,534, AVeriTeC at 4,568, again none of them numerically focused. StatProps is the one prior dataset with a numerical focus, and it is synthetic, generated by rule from 16 statistical properties of geographic regions in Freebase. QuanTemp is the only row with a check mark in both the Numerical Focus and Unleaked Evidence columns, and its 423,320-snippet corpus is the largest among the fact-checker-sourced datasets by a factor of three.

Figure 3 shows the segmenter on one claim: “During paul’s 29 seasons as chairman of the chicago bulls, the team captured the title seven times, including in 2000.” Three subtrees survive. “29 seasons” and “seven times” each resolve to a noun phrase over a cardinal number and a plural noun, CD plus NNS. The middle one is tagged NP-TMP, a temporal noun phrase, which is how a duration is distinguished from a count. “2000” resolves to a noun phrase over a bare CD. The claim needs all three quantities to verify, and the tree is what tells the pipeline that.

QuanTemp dataset distribution. Table 5 from the paper [1].
Split True False Conflicting Total
Train 1,824 5,770 2,341 9,935
Dev 617 1,795 672 3,084
Test 474 1,423 598 2,495

The splits are unbalanced in the same direction at every level, roughly 58% False throughout, which the authors attribute to fact-checkers choosing what to fact-check. Every reported number should be read against the majority-class baseline this produces: 24.21 macro-F1 and 41.42 weighted-F1.

A separate weak-supervision pass sorts the claims into four numerical categories, so that a failure can be attributed to a specific kind of reasoning. Fifty claims were annotated by hand, gpt-3.5-turbo labelled a few hundred more from those as in-context examples, and a SetFit classifier trained on the result labelled the rest. Two annotators checked 250 random claims and agreed with 199 of the assignments, an accuracy of 80%.

Claim categories and their distribution. Counts and shares from Table 6 of the paper [1].
Category Claims Share Requires
Statistical 7,302 47.07% a quantity or statistic looked up and compared
Temporal 4,193 27.03% a date or duration resolved
Interval 2,357 15.19% reasoning over a range of values
Comparison 1,645 10.60% two quantities compared against each other

Results

Every experiment holds the retrieval stack fixed and varies one component at a time. Three components get varied across the two tables:

  • Held fixed: the retrieval stack. BM25 returns the top 100 documents per query and paraphrase-MiniLM-L6-v2 re-ranks them, with the top 3 snippets passed on. The authors swept and found 3 best at claim level.
  • Held fixed: three snippets per claim. The no-decomposition condition takes the claim’s top 3, the two decomposition conditions take the top 1 per question, so all three see the same amount of evidence.
  • Varied in Table 7: the query. The raw claim, ClaimDecomp’s sub-questions, or Program-FC’s program. The verdict model stays at Roberta-Large-MNLI throughout these three rows: a three-class classifier reading the claim, the questions, and the evidence concatenated with separators, fine-tuned to early stopping with patience 2, batch size 16, and AdamW at a learning rate of .
  • Varied in Table 7: the evidence source. The lower block swaps the retrieved snippets for the fact-checkers’ own justification paragraphs, then swaps the training set from numerical claims alone to a mix of numerical and non-numerical ones.
  • Varied in Table 8: the verdict model. Eight replacements over ten rows, with the query held at ClaimDecomp. Two of the eight appear twice, once zero-shot and once few-shot.
    • Fine-tuned. bart-large-mnli, Roberta-large, T5-small, NumT5-small [7], and FinQA-Roberta-Large [8]. The last two are the middle two with numerical pretraining added, so NumT5-small against T5-small and FinQA-Roberta-Large against Roberta-large each isolate that one factor.
    • Prompted. flan-t5-xl and gpt-3.5-turbo in both zero-shot and few-shot settings, GPT-4 few-shot only, all at temperature 0.3 and asked for a verdict and a justification together.
  • Scoring. Macro-F1 and weighted-F1 over the 2,495-claim test set, plus per-class F1 and a breakdown by the four numerical categories. Significance is a t-test at the 0.01 level, measured against the raw-claim baseline in Table 7 and against Roberta-large in Table 8.

The findings:

  • Decomposition beats using the claim as the query (Table 7). ClaimDecomp reaches 57.12 macro-F1 and 64.89 weighted-F1 against 52.48 and 58.52 for the raw claim, relative gains of 8.84% and 10.9%, both significant at 0.01. Program-FC reaches 53.43 macro-F1, between the two, and does not reach significance.
  • The gain concentrates on the Conflicting class (Table 7). Conflicting-class F1 moves from 35.27 to 39.72 under ClaimDecomp. These are the claims that are partly right, so the verdict needs evidence pulling in two directions, and a single query built from the whole claim tends to return one side of it or nothing at all.
  • Comparison claims gain the most (Table 7). 53.59 against 40.72 macro-F1, a relative gain of 31.6%, and 34.7% on weighted-F1. Interval claims gain second-most, 56.02 against 48.84. Temporal claims are both the easiest category in absolute terms and the least improved, 61.46 against 60.29.
  • Better questions, measured directly (Tables 9 and 10). ClaimDecomp’s questions score 0.831 on BERTScore relevance against Program-FC’s 0.782, and 0.490 against 0.430 on a diversity measure built from 1−BLEU plus Word Position Deviation. Two annotators rating 20 sampled claims on a 1–5 scale put ClaimDecomp ahead on question usefulness, 3.7 against 3.4, and on evidence usefulness, 3.2 against 2.9. Program-FC leads only on completeness, 4.6 against 4.5.
  • Number-pretrained NLI models beat their general-purpose twins (Table 8). NumT5-small [7] reaches 50.26 macro-F1 against T5-small’s 44.96, a relative gain of 11.8%. FinQA-Roberta-Large [8] reaches 58.32 against Roberta-large’s 54.43, a relative gain of 7.1%, and that 58.32 is the paper’s headline number. It is also the only configuration to push Conflicting-class F1 past 47.
  • Prompting trails fine-tuning (Table 8). gpt-3.5-turbo few-shot reaches 47.00 macro-F1 and GPT-4 few-shot 36.50, against 54.43 for a fine-tuned 355M-parameter encoder. GPT-4 few-shot scores below the fine-tuned 60M-parameter T5-small. Zero-shot is worse still: FlanT5 at 30.68 and gpt-3.5-turbo at 33.87. The authors attribute the gap to the models misreading evidence they have parsed correctly.
  • Gold evidence raises the ceiling without lifting it far (Table 7). Fine-tuning on the fact-checkers’ own justification paragraphs reaches 62.85 macro-F1 and 69.79 weighted-F1. Training on a mix of numerical and non-numerical claims from the same fact-checkers drops that to 58.66 and 66.73, a fall of 7.14% in macro-F1, which is the paper’s evidence that numerical claims are their own distribution rather than a slice of a general one.

My Notes

  • QuanTemp’s corpus can contain evidence written after the claim was checked: the searches ran in late 2023 against claims fact-checked years earlier, and nothing filters a snippet by publication date. AVeriTeC [2] controls for this. Its annotators search a Google bar restricted to documents published before the claim date, and its splits are temporally disjoint. Table 1 still gives QuanTemp the check mark in Unleaked Evidence and AVeriTeC a cross, because a footnote restricts the column to “gold evidence being leaked from fact-checking websites.” So the column covers one kind of leakage and not the other, and the two datasets each avoid a different one. A reader who takes the check mark at face value will credit QuanTemp with both. The follow-up from two of the same authors, QuanTemp++ [9], admits the temporal problem in its own abstract: existing benchmarks use “weakly supervised web search to collect evidences… with temporal leakage rendering a less realistic retrieval setting.”
  • The paper never scores the evidence it retrieves: there is no recall@k, no nDCG, no retrieval number anywhere in it, because the dataset includes no relevance labels. Retrieval quality is measured once, as a 1–5 usefulness rating on 20 sampled claims, which came out at 2.9 and 3.2, near the middle of the scale. So when Table 8 compares eight verdict models over ten rows, a reader cannot tell whether FinQA-Roberta-Large’s 3.89-point macro-F1 lead over Roberta-large comes from better numerical reasoning or from coping better with the same noisy snippets. FEVER-based work does not have this problem, because FEVER annotates evidence at sentence level, so From Relevance to Utility [10] can report retrieval precision, recall, and F1 at five sentences alongside verdict accuracy. QuanTemp++ fixes that, releasing per-claim relevance judgments with a pre-indexed corpus.
  • Two fixes to the verdict model failed in the follow-up shared task: QuanTemp became Task 3 of the CLEF 2025 CheckThat! lab, whose organizers include two of the authors here [11]. CheckThat! 2026 then extended numerical claim verification to English and Arabic [12]. One top-four 2025 system tried a longer context window with more retrieved snippets, and right-to-left tokenization, which helps arithmetic reasoning. Neither helped numerical entailment. Heil and Pramov scored 0.57 macro-F1 [13], close to the 58.32 here, though the task supplied claims rather than the paper’s corpus, so participants built their own retrieval and the two numbers are not a like-for-like comparison. The same pattern is in the paper’s own numbers: replacing the retrieved snippets with the fact-checkers’ justification paragraphs is worth 5.73 macro-F1 points, more than any verdict model in Table 8 gained.

References

  1. item.title: The 2nd AVeriTeC Shared Task: Open-Weights, Reproducible and Efficient Systems
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

In The 2nd Automated Verification of Textual Claims (AVeriTeC) Shared Task: Open-weights, Reproducible and Efficient Systems [1] (the Eighth Fact Extraction and VERification workshop, FEVER, at ACL 2025 in Vienna, July 2025), Mubashara Akhtar (ETH Zurich), Rami Aly, Yulong Chen, Zhenyun Deng (Cambridge), Michael Schlichtkrull (Cambridge and Queen Mary University of London), Chenxi Whitehouse (Cambridge and Meta), and Andreas Vlachos (Cambridge) report the second edition of the shared task built on the AVeriTeC claim-verification dataset [2]. Where the first edition [3] was won by systems calling commercial language-model APIs, this one bars external calls at inference time: every system must run on a single 23 GB GPU, finish a claim in a minute, and retrieve its evidence from a knowledge store the organizers compiled in advance.

Two measurements decide the leaderboard:

  • AVeriTeC score: verdict accuracy, counted only for claims where the system’s retrieved evidence clears a similarity threshold against the annotators’ gold evidence. A system that labels a claim correctly off the wrong evidence scores zero on it, so the number is a joint retrieval-and-verdict measure rather than an accuracy figure.
  • Ev2R recall: the evidence-similarity component, new this year [4]. An LLM-as-judge decomposes both the retrieved and the reference evidence into atomic facts, then measures what share of the reference facts the retrieved evidence supports. It is reported twice, over questions alone (Q only) and over question-answer pairs (Q + A), and the second one gates the AVeriTeC score. Both column names come from the dataset paper, where they scored token overlap, so the figures do not compare across the two.

In the First Automated Verification of Textual Claims (AVeriTeC) shared task, participating teams developed systems that for each claim retrieve evidence from the web and predict its veracity. While there was progress in automated fact-checking for real-world claims, the majority of the systems proposed relied on large closed-weights language models, which rendered them expensive to run and less reproducible. To ameliorate this issue, in this year’s edition of the AVeriTeC shared task, we required system to use only open-weights models that could be run using a single GPU with 23GBs of RAM, and that systems should take one minute or less to return verdicts accompanied by evidence retrieved from a pre-compiled knowledge store. The shared task received 7 submissions; 6 of which exceeded the accuracy of our baseline on the test set, while they ran in under a minute per claim on the hardware we had specified. The winning team was CTU AIC with an AVeriTeC score of 33.17%. In this paper we describe the shared task in detail and highlight key findings.

Methods

The task itself is inherited from the dataset: given a claim plus metadata such as speaker and date, retrieve supporting or refuting evidence, then assign one of four verdicts: Supported, Refuted, Not Enough Evidence, or Conflicting Evidence/Cherry-picking. Gold evidence is annotated as question-answer pairs, a format the authors note accommodates multi-hop reasoning. Systems were not required to answer in it, though most did.

Four pieces of infrastructure define this edition:

  • A fresh test set. 1,000 new claims running from January to December 2024.
    • Annotation. The same five-phase pipeline as the original dataset: extract and decontextualise the claim, generate question-answer pairs and a verdict, then have a different annotator produce a verdict from the question-answer pairs alone.
    • Adjudication. A claim is admitted when those two verdicts agree. Disagreement sends it through a second round of both steps with fresh annotators, and a second disagreement discards it.
    • Annotator qualification. Clearing 70% F1 on claim-type and fact-checking-strategy classification, more than two question-answer pairs per claim, and 50% verdict accuracy on training instances. 8 of 9 candidates passed.
    • Difficulty. The 2025 claims average 2.79 questions each and are further from the training data than any earlier split, the largest domain shift of the three test sets.
  • A pre-compiled knowledge store. The frozen evidence pool, in place of live web search.
    • Construction. For each claim the organizers assembled the gold documents plus Google results for machine-generated queries, including distractor queries built by swapping the claim’s named entities, dates, and events, keeping only URLs available before the claim was made. Each URL’s text is then scraped with trafilatura, so a system reads extracted article text rather than raw HTML.
    • Size. 1,018,800 URLs and roughly 2.5 billion tokens: about 1,019 URLs per claim, of which 593 have usable scraped text.
    • Effect. Two systems are compared over the same evidence pool, and nobody pays for search.
  • A fixed inference environment. One machine, on which the organizers ran every submitted system against the hidden test set.
    • Hardware. An AWS g5.2xlarge instance, meaning one Nvidia A10G with 23 GB of GPU memory, 8 vCPUs, and 32 GB of system RAM.
    • Reproducibility. A system counts as reproducible if it completes inference there with no external API calls, so closed-weights models are excluded at inference but allowed during training.
    • Efficiency. The budget is 16 hours 40 minutes for 1,000 claims, a minute per claim on average. Systems were permitted to run one pipeline stage across all claims before starting the next, which sidesteps repeated model loading.
    • Effect on the ranking. None. Both reproducibility and efficiency are pass/fail admission gates.
  • A new evidence metric. Ev2R, in place of last year’s token overlap.
    • What it replaces. Last year’s scoring compared generated and gold question-answer pairs by token overlap with METEOR [5], which penalises valid evidence phrased differently from the annotator’s and which correlated near zero with human judgment.
    • Recall only. Only Ev2R’s recall half is used, so a system is not punished for returning extra context the annotators skipped.
    • Capped at 10 questions. Only a system’s first 10 questions count, so volume alone earns nothing.
    • The gate. The AVeriTeC score is verdict accuracy conditioned on Ev2R recall above .

Table 1 sets the 2025 test set beside the original 2023 splits and last year’s test set: claim counts, questions per claim, the date of the last claim, and percentage breakdowns by verdict, by claim type, and by the strategy the fact-checker used. The 2025 claims end on 19 December 2024. Numerical claims make up 38.8% of them and causal claims 8.1%, a shift the authors describe as easing verification, since they call numerical claims the more straightforward kind and causal claims the harder one.

The baseline is HerO [6], the runner-up from the first edition, cut down to fit the budget: Llama-3.1-8B in place of the 70B model throughout, BM25 retrieval capped at 5,000 sentences and reranking at 500, plus batching and multithreading.

Results

Seven of eight submissions ran. The findings:

  • Six of seven systems beat the baseline. The ranking is the cover table’s AVeriTeC score column. Team CTU AIC won with 0.3317 [7], ahead of HUMANE at 0.2707 and Yellow Flash at 0.2527. The baseline scored 0.2023, and only OldJoe fell below it, at 0.1517. Every system also cleared the runtime budget, from EFC at 7.01 seconds per claim to CTU AIC at 53.67.
  • Reproducible meant reproducible-after-repair. One of the eight submissions never ran, defeated by syntax errors, missing installation instructions, and hardcoded paths. All seven that did run needed manual intervention first: Docker permission errors, dependency build failures, GPU memory crashes, and misconfigured shell scripts, each resolved inside four hours. The organizers also monitored network traffic for non-local calls and ran every system on 99 held-out claims to catch hardcoding against the test set.
  • The field converged on two model families. Every generative stage across all seven systems runs on Qwen3, Qwen2.5, or Phi-4, at 14B parameters or below except HUMANE’s fine-tuned Qwen3-32B verdict head, while retrieval runs on BM25 and open embedding models. Five systems serve with vLLM, one with llama.cpp, and the winner with Ollama. Fine-tuning was rare: only HUMANE and FZIGOT trained anything, the latter using low-rank adapters [8] on weakly supervised data for three separate pipeline stages.
  • Quantization was near-universal, and the winner declined it. Every non-baseline system except CTU AIC compressed its weights to fit the 23 GB card. CTU AIC instead ran the largest model and context window it could fit uncompressed, which made it the slowest system on the board and the most accurate. EFC went the other way: a filtering step that predicts Not Enough Evidence and Conflicting Evidence/Cherry-picking from cosine similarity alone, skipping the language-model call, got it to roughly five times the baseline’s speed at a score just above it, 0.2047 against 0.2023.
  • The top systems skip explicit question generation. CTU AIC retrieves on the bare claim and generates questions, answers, and verdict together afterwards, while HUMANE expands the query into a hypothetical fact-checking article first. Both outrank the five systems that generate questions up front, and neither leads the question-only column: the highest Q-only recall belongs to FZIGOT at 0.3622 in 4th place, with the baseline second on that column at 0.2723 while placing 7th, against the winner’s 0.2003. The knowledge store, though, was itself built from generated queries. Their 20-claim probe finds complete evidence for 6 claims when searching the claim alone, against 19 under the full query-construction process, so question generation is doing the work one layer down.
  • Numerical claims are the hardest type. Averaged over systems, numerical claims score 0.16, against 0.25 for quote verification, 0.30 for both event/property and causal claims, and 0.36 for position statements. The organizers had described the 2025 test set’s tilt toward numerical claims (38.8%) as a tilt toward claims “more straightforward to verify,” and its smaller share of causal claims (8.1%) as fewer of the “typically more challenging” kind. The authors suggest the widened gap since the first edition is likely down to the change of metric.
  • Two verdict labels are effectively unsolved. On Not Enough Evidence no system exceeds 0.10, and on Conflicting Evidence/Cherry-picking none exceeds 0.06. Several teams dropped those two labels from their output entirely.
  • Human raters rate relevance high and coverage low. Six of the seven teams plus two outside annotators rated evidence samples on a 1–5 scale for relevance to the claim and for coverage of the reference evidence, 35 samples each, leaving 198 valid annotations once the gold-labelled and unusable ones were dropped. About 79% are 4 or 5 for relevance, while coverage is spread almost uniformly, with 17.7% at 1 and 23.7% at 2. Ev2R correlates with the human coverage rating at Spearman and with relevance at , against roughly zero for last year’s token-matching metric, and the human ranking of teams broadly reproduces the leaderboard.
  • A closed-model swap lowered the winner’s score. The organizers reran CTU AIC’s pipeline with GPT-4o and GPT-4o-mini in place of Qwen3-14B. Q-only recall rose sharply, to 0.5035 and 0.5718 against 0.2003, while Q+A recall and the AVeriTeC score both fell, with GPT-4o-mini beating GPT-4o. The authors call this preliminary, since neither substitution was tuned for their pipeline.

My Notes

  • The benchmark is drifting toward its majority class: Refuted is 62.0% of the 2023 test set, 66.5% of 2024’s, and 71.9% of 2025’s, while Conflicting Evidence/Cherry-picking falls 6.3% → 4.1% → 1.7% (Table 1). At 1.7% that second label covers 17 of 1,000 claims, too few to score a system on, which explains the near-empty column in Table 4. The same label separated AVeriTeC from three-way benchmarks. The organizers note that systems are rewarded for calibrating toward Refuted, and the reward grows as the Refuted share grows. The claims come from what fact-checking organizations chose to publish, so the cause may be a shift in what gets fact-checked.
  • The score rewards matching the annotators’ sources: Ev2R recall measures how much of the annotators’ evidence is covered by the system’s evidence, fact by fact. A system that reaches the right verdict through different but equally sound sources scores low. In the human evaluation, samples the raters gave 5 on relevance, with the same verdict as the reference, scored low on coverage because the wording and sources differed. From Relevance to Utility [9] attacks the same gap at training time, where a retriever tuned on the verifier’s feedback beats one tuned on relevance labels. A sufficiency test would fit the task better: does this evidence support the gold verdict, regardless of which sources it came from.
  • Numbers are where the judge is least reliable: the organizers attribute the widened gap to the metric change, but causal claims score 0.30, tied for second, and causal is the type they deemed more challenging. If switching to Ev2R had depressed hard types generally, causal should have fallen too. Numerical reference evidence splits into many precise atomic facts, and a passage can state the right conclusion while missing most of the figures, so the recall term is the likely cause of the low numerical scores. Ev2R also fails the other way: the human evaluation flags a top-ranked sample whose “predicted evidence directly contradicts the reference evidence by providing different numbers, yet it receives a high AVeriTeC score due to similar wording” (Table 10, row three).
  • Leakage would hit every system at once: the limitations section flags that Qwen3’s training cutoff is estimated at March 2025 while the test claims run through December 2024, so leakage is possible. The 23 GB limit narrowed everyone’s model choices. Six of the seven teams generate questions with a Qwen model and four run one for the verdict, with Phi-4-14B in the other three (Table 3). Leakage in Qwen’s pretraining data would then move most of the board together, and a ranking between two Qwen-based systems cannot separate memorised claims from retrieved evidence. Refreshing the test set each year only helps while the new claims postdate the models’ cutoffs, and this edition’s do not. The organizers suggest requiring open training data as well as open weights, which would let anyone check.
  • The successor edition made the store optional: the group’s image-text dataset AVerImaTeC [10] got its own shared task at FEVER 2026 [11], run by four of the organizers here, and participants may use the provided knowledge store, their own search engines, or both. The stated reason for supplying a store is now the cost of web-search APIs. So the constraint the 2025 edition was built around held for one round. Ev2R carried over, extended to multimodal evidence.

item.title: Recursive Language Models vs. Subagents: A Primer
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

A language model has a fixed context window. Long before that window is full, its answers start to degrade. Once a job outgrows the range where the model stays reliable, the work has to be split across several model calls. Two families of systems disagree about what gets split.

Subagents split the task. A lead model reads the request, decides what the pieces are, writes each piece out as an instruction in plain English, hands it to a fresh copy of the model, and combines what comes back.

Recursive language models (RLMs) split the input. The model never receives the long text at all. The text is parked in a Python session as a variable, and the model writes code that peeks at it, cuts it up, and calls itself on whichever pieces need a model’s judgment rather than a regular expression.

Both patterns date from 2025, both now have a year of published results, and both have picked up their own skeptical literature. This primer covers what subagents and RLMs each are, what the evidence shows, what the comparison means if you are building on either, and how the two designs are merging.

Why performance drops as inputs grow

Every long-context method exists because of one observation: models get worse as their input gets longer, and they get worse long before the input is too big to accept. Chroma named this context rot in a July 2025 technical report [2]. The standard test, needle in a haystack, buries a known sentence in a pile of irrelevant text and asks the model to find it. Frontier models score near-perfectly, which invites the conclusion that long context is solved. But that test is lexical matching.

Chroma changed four things about it. They varied the needle to require a semantic rather than a word-for-word match, added plausible distractors, ran a conversational question-answer benchmark, and asked models to reproduce a series of repeated words. Performance fell off with input length in every case, and fell off unevenly.

Nobody has a settled explanation for why. Alex Zhang, the first author of the RLM work, says the most plausible one is that long sequences are simply rare in training data, so the far end of a context window is out of distribution.

Subagents: split the task

Picture a manager with four research assistants. The manager reads the brief, writes four short assignments, and hands one to each assistant. Each assistant goes off, reads a pile of documents nobody else sees, and comes back with a one-page memo. The manager reads four memos and writes the answer. The manager never reads the documents.

That is the whole idea. Anthropic’s engineering write-up on Claude’s Research feature states the reason plainly: “The essence of search is compression: distilling insights from a vast corpus” [4]. A subagent may burn tens of thousands of tokens exploring, then hand back a summary of one or two thousand [5]. The lead agent’s context fills up with memos while the evidence stays behind in the subagents.

Anthropic’s system uses an orchestrator-worker pattern: a lead agent plans, spawns subagents that search in parallel, and synthesizes their returns. Two numbers from that post are the reason the pattern spread. A lead Claude Opus 4 with Claude Sonnet 4 subagents beat single-agent Claude Opus 4 by 90.2% on Anthropic’s internal research eval. Then, on BrowseComp, a benchmark for finding hard-to-locate information on the web, they looked at what separated their successful runs from their failed ones. How many tokens a run spent accounted for 80% of the difference all by itself. Adding two more factors, the number of tool calls and which model was used, brought the total to 95% [4].

The second number explains the first. Subagents work largely because they are a way to spend more tokens on a problem than one context window can hold. The bill matches: Anthropic reports that agents use roughly 4× the tokens of a chat interaction, and multi-agent systems roughly 15× [4].

The pattern is now a default. Claude Code offers subagents as a built-in feature, and LangChain’s Deep Agents packages planning plus subagents plus a filesystem as a library (post).

Recursive language models: split the input

Now picture a different assistant. You hand this one a 10,000-page archive and a question. Instead of reading, the assistant writes a short script. Print the first page to see how the thing is formatted. Search for the twelve lines that mention the right date range. Cut the file at the chapter breaks, and for each of the 200 chapters, ask a colleague “does anything here mention X?” The archive is never read by the assistant, only by the script.

That is an RLM, proposed in October 2025 by Alex Zhang, Tim Kraska, and Omar Khattab at MIT CSAIL [1], [6]. The mechanics are small enough to state in full:

  • The prompt becomes a variable. The long input is loaded into a sandboxed Python read-eval-print loop (REPL) as a string in memory. The root model, which the paper calls depth 0, starts out knowing only the question and the size of that string.
  • The model writes code, and sees only what the code prints. print(prompt[:100]) to peek. prompt.split("Chapter 2") to cut. A regular expression to filter. Whatever the code prints comes back into the model’s context.
  • The model can call itself as a function. An llm_query() call inside the REPL hands a slice of the input to a fresh copy of the model, a sub-call at depth 1. The sub-call’s answer comes back as an ordinary Python value.
  • From outside, an RLM looks like one model call. The paper presents rlm.completion(messages) as a drop-in replacement for gpt5.completion(messages). What the caller gets back is a single completion, with the agent loop hidden inside it.

Reading actual RLM trajectories, the authors found a small set of recurring behaviors [6]:

  • Peeking: grab the first couple thousand characters to learn the format, the way a programmer inspects the head of an unfamiliar dataset.
  • Grepping: narrow with keywords or a regular expression instead of a retrieval model.
  • Partition and map: chunk the input and fire a sub-call at each chunk, for the cases where no pattern match will do because the thing being looked for is semantic.
  • Summarizing: condense regions of the input for the root model to reason over, which makes ordinary compaction one thing an RLM can choose to do.
  • Stitching long outputs: solve each piece with a sub-call and concatenate, which turns tasks like “produce the final file after 400 diffs” into a programming problem instead of a generation problem.

Delegating in prose vs. delegating in code

Both approaches make many model calls. Both keep the long material out of the top-level context. So it is fair to ask whether an RLM is a subagent system with extra steps. The RLM paper answers in one sentence in its introduction:

Similarly, prior self-delegation approaches […] allow LLMs to invoke themselves as sub-agents. However, they are handicapped by the underlying LLM’s limited output lengths because they are designed to verbalize sub-calls autoregressively rather than producing them programmatically.

In plainer terms: a subagent orchestrator has to type out every delegation. Ten subagents cost ten paragraphs of written instructions, and a thousand cost a thousand, which no output budget allows. An RLM writes a for loop. A thousand sub-calls cost the same dozen tokens as ten, because the model emits the rule rather than the instances.

The second difference is easy to overstate, and the RLM authors do overstate it. Zhang closes the original post this way:

Agents are designed based on human / expert intuition on how to break down a problem to be digestible for an LM. RLMs are designed based on the principle that fundamentally, LMs should decide how to break down a problem to be digestible for an LM.

That is true of fixed-topology multi-agent systems, where a person wires up a searcher, a verifier, and a writer in advance. It is not true of the orchestrator-worker systems that made the pattern popular. Anthropic’s lead agent is itself a language model, and it picks the split per query: “the lead agent analyzes it, develops a strategy, and spawns subagents to explore different aspects simultaneously” [4]. The best evidence that the model rather than a person is choosing is the failure mode Anthropic reports, early agents “spawning 50 subagents for simple queries.” A human designer does not accidentally choose 50. ClawArena-Team exists for the same reason: it measures how well a model manages a team, which only makes sense as a question if the model is the one deciding [7].

A person fixes less than Zhang suggests. Anthropic describes its own contribution as “instilling good heuristics rather than rigid rules,” encoding into the lead agent’s prompt what skilled human researchers do, including when to go deep and when to go wide [4]. The human sets the guidance and the vocabulary of delegation. The model still makes the call.

What differs is how many splits each one can afford to consider. Because each prose delegation costs a paragraph, a lead agent can only pick among a handful of coarse assignments, and those tend to resemble the roles its prompt described. Because a code delegation costs a line, an RLM can express splits nobody enumerated: chunk into 200 pieces, filter by pattern first and call the model only on what survives, or set the chunk size from what the opening peek showed about the format.

Subagents RLMs
What gets split The task The input
Who chooses the split The lead model, guided by a human-written prompt The model, in code it writes for that query
Range of splits available A handful of prose assignments Any program over the input
How a delegation is expressed A prose instruction A line of code
Cost of 1,000 delegations 1,000 written instructions One loop
What the top-level context holds Returned summaries Printed output of its own code
What the caller sees An agent run One completion
Fails when Subagents make conflicting assumptions The model cannot write good code

The evidence on subagents

The case for is largely the Anthropic result above, plus the hierarchical variants that followed it. Matryoshka Agent applies the same orchestrator-and-workers split to machine-learning engineering, where an orchestrator keeps a compact record of what has been explored while subagents run the expensive attempts, and reports up to a 36.7% relative gain on Qwen3-30B-Coder [8]. Its orchestrator built on Qwen3-4B-Instruct reaches performance comparable to o4-mini, which is a hint about where model capacity has to go.

The case against arrived quickly, and in three flavors.

The first is architectural, from Cognition, which builds Devin. Its June 2025 position piece, “Don’t Build Multi-Agents,” argues from two principles [9]:

Share context, and share full agent traces, not just individual messages

Actions carry implicit decisions, and conflicting decisions carry bad results

The illustration is a request to clone Flappy Bird, split between a subagent building the bird and a subagent building the background. Both do competent work and the results do not match, because each made a visual-style decision the other never saw. Passing the original task down does not fix it, since the decisions that matter were made in tool calls and turns that no summary preserves. Cognition’s recommendation is a single-threaded agent with a dedicated model, in their case fine-tuned, whose only job is compressing history into decisions and events [9].

The second is empirical. “The Illusion of Multi-Agent Advantage” evaluated automatically designed multi-agent systems against a plain single-agent baseline, chain-of-thought with self-consistency, and found the multi-agent systems consistently behind despite costing up to 10× as much [10]. On a synthetic dataset built specifically to have the properties multi-agent systems are supposed to exploit, decomposable tasks with separable contexts, expert-designed architectures beat automatically generated ones on both accuracy and cost. The authors’ reading is that automated design produces complexity that does not do anything.

The third is theoretical, and it reconciles the first two with Anthropic’s 90.2%. “When Do Multi-Agent Systems Help? An Information Bottleneck Perspective” observes that a single agent accumulates one shared trace, while a multi-agent system has isolated local contexts joined by bounded relay messages [11]. With unbounded relays a multi-agent system can just forward everything and reproduce the single agent exactly, so any real advantage has to come from the compression the bounded relay forces. The trade is between dropping redundant context, which helps, and dropping task-relevant context, which hurts. The authors back this with 18 controlled experiments, spanning five benchmarks and three sizes of model. Multi-agent systems help when the relay loses little, and help most for weaker models. The gains shrink or reverse for stronger models that were already capable of using the redundant context themselves.

The prediction that falls out of this is that as base models improve, the delegation tax gets harder to justify at fixed relay bandwidth.

A newer line of work asks whether a model can run a team at all. ClawArena-Team measures the management ability of the lead model specifically, holding the subagent pool fixed so score differences reflect orchestration rather than raw capability [7]. The setup deliberately handicaps the manager: it reads only text, and it can reach only part of the workspace directly, so anything else has to go through a subagent. That forces two separate skills. Modality routing is sending an image-grounded question to a worker that can actually see images rather than guessing from the surrounding text. Least-privilege empowerment is granting each subagent only the tools and file paths its assignment needs, so that a worker which misbehaves cannot reach anything else.

Models turn out to be adequate at the first and poor at the second. No model exceeded 50% workspace-permission precision, meaning that more than half the access each manager handed out was access the assignment never called for. The managers were not failing to see what a subagent needed. They were failing to withhold what it did not, which is the same over-permissioning problem that ordinary software security spends most of its effort on.

Paying more does not buy better management. API cost across the twelve models varied by more than 100×, while overall scores varied by less than 4×, and the cheapest open models were among the most efficient. The scores also make the models look more alike than they are. Most land inside a 9.9-point band. But among the capable ones, how often a subagent reached a path it should not have varied by about 12×.

The evidence on RLMs

Start with the strongest numbers. On four long-context tasks with GPT-5, the RLM beats common scaffolds by a median of 26% against compaction, 130% against CodeAct with sub-calls, and 13% against Claude Code, at comparable cost, and it keeps working past 10M tokens. The individual entries in Table 1 are more informative than the medians [1]:

  • On BrowseComp-Plus at 6M to 11M tokens [12], a version of BrowseComp where every candidate document is supplied up front instead of searched for on the web, plain GPT-5 scores 0.0 because the input does not fit. The RLM scores 91.3, rising to 92.0 at greater recursion depth. It is not the best number in that column: OpenCode with the context offloaded to a file reaches 94.0.
  • On OOLONG-Pairs, a synthetic pairwise-reasoning task the RLM authors built at only 32K tokens, well inside every window involved, GPT-5 scores 0.1, OpenCode with offloading 4.8, and Claude Code with offloading 6.5. The RLM scores 58.0. Capacity cannot explain this one, since everything fit.
  • On code-repository question answering, the ordering is much tighter: 62.0 for the RLM against 64.0 for OpenCode with offloading. The Claude Code rows are not a like-for-like comparison, since the paper runs that baseline on Claude Opus 4.1 rather than GPT-5.

One finding argues against the method’s own name. Recursion is not where most of the gain comes from. The paper’s own ablation at depth 0, meaning the REPL with no sub-calls at all, already reaches 88.0 of the RLM’s 91.3 on BrowseComp-Plus. With Qwen3-Coder-480B-A35B on code question answering, depth 0 at 66.0 beats depth 1 at 56.0. And depth does not increase monotonically once it is switched on: with GPT-5, code question answering runs 58.0, 62.0, 66.0, 58.0 across depths 0 through 3, while OOLONG-Pairs climbs steadily, 43.9, 58.0, 65.5, 76.0 [1].

Two independent follow-ups turn that observation into a claim.

  • A reproduction study ran depth 1 and depth 2 on open agentic models and found deeper recursion made models “overthink”: accuracy dropped on simple retrieval, and one execution went from 3.6 seconds to 344.5 seconds [13].
  • SRLM keeps the REPL and drops the recursion requirement, replacing it with sampling eight candidate programs and picking one using the model’s own uncertainty signals. SRLM reports gains up to 22% over RLM under a matched time budget, and finds that RLMs with recursion often score below the base model for inputs that fit in the window. The paper states directly that recursion is not the primary driver of RLM performance (post) [14].

Taken with the depth-0 rows in the original paper, the reasonable summary is narrower than the method’s name suggests. Programmatic access to the input is doing most of the work. Recursive sub-calls are a specialized tool, and they pay off on inputs where the thing being looked for is semantic rather than findable by pattern.

The paper’s negative-results appendix records what did not work [1]:

  • The method needs a competent coding model. Qwen3-8B struggled as an RLM because it could not reason well enough in a REPL.
  • Thinking models can run out of output tokens. Several Qwen3-235B-A22B trajectories hit the per-call output limit mid-run because reasoning tokens consumed the budget, which is why its gains fell below those of the two models in the main results.
  • The prompt does not transfer between models. Qwen3-Coder had to be explicitly warned not to over-delegate, or it would issue thousands of sub-calls on basic tasks.
  • Every sub-call blocks. The published implementation issues them one after another with no prefix caching, which can make an RLM slower than the base model it wraps.
  • A text tag is the only signal that an answer is final. The model is asked to wrap a finished answer in a FINAL() tag, and the loop stops when it sees one. Models sometimes put a plan inside the tag instead, which ends the run on a plan.

Designs that combine both

Nothing so far settles whether to split the task or split the input. The newest designs do both.

“Recursive Agent Harnesses” names the pattern in between [15]. Keep the RLM idea that delegations are emitted as code, but let each recursive unit be a whole agent, with its own tools, sandbox, and plan, instead of a bare model call. A parent agent writes a script, runs it, and gets many child agents working at once on the repetitive parts, reserving plain function calls for the small ones. The authors ran this with the backbone pinned to GPT-5 so it matched the Codex and RLM numbers already published, which lets them credit the difference to the harness instead of the model: a Codex baseline of 71.75% rose to 81.36% on a long-context aggregation benchmark reaching 4M tokens. Swapping in Claude Sonnet 4.5 took the same design to 89.77%.

The same pattern is now in production. In Claude Code’s dynamic workflows, Claude writes an orchestration script and a background runtime executes it, running up to 16 agents at once and up to 1,000 across a single run [16] (post). The documentation draws the same distinction the RLM paper drew, in nearly the same terms:

A workflow moves the plan into code. With subagents, skills, and agent teams, Claude is the orchestrator: it decides turn by turn what to spawn or assign next, and every result lands in a context window. A workflow script holds the loop, the branching, and the intermediate results itself, so Claude’s context holds only the final answer.

Chained RLM comes at the merger from the other side. That design replaces a single long trajectory with a sequence of fresh roots, each inheriting a compact summary, a shared plain-text blackboard, and durable artifacts written by its predecessors rather than the full conversation [17].

All three designs make the same two choices: emit delegations as code rather than prose, and make whatever receives a delegation as capable as the task requires.

Practical implications

  • Ask which thing is too big, the task or the input: one long object, a repository, a corpus, a transcript, a log file, points to splitting the input. Several genuinely independent lines of inquiry, each needing its own search, points to splitting the task. Most real work has some of each, which is what the merged designs above are for.
  • A REPL over the input is the cheap first move: the depth-0 results and SRLM both say most of the benefit comes from letting the model manipulate the long input programmatically. A sandboxed REPL is much less machinery than an orchestration layer, and it can come first.
  • The input split needs a model that codes well: RLM-style methods put the whole burden on coding ability, and on a weak base model the pattern degrades. The information-bottleneck result points the other way for weak models, where the compression a prose relay forces is what helps most.
  • Budget in tokens rather than wall clock: Anthropic’s 15× multiplier and SRLM’s eight parallel programs are both real costs that a latency measurement hides. Running eight programs at once shortens the wait without reducing the bill.
  • Both families fail at the joins: the MAST taxonomy puts a whole category of multi-agent failures at inter-agent misalignment (post) [18]. The RLM failures the authors list are handoff problems too, an answer mistaken for a plan, a syntax error in generated code. Instrument the handoffs.
  • Put the strongest model in the manager seat: a controlled sweep over hierarchical search agents scaled each role on its own and found that a bigger delegating model improved exact match by about 11 points, while a bigger execution subagent moved it about 2.6 [19]. The workers can be cheap. A 1.7B executor trained on filtered trajectories matched a frontier subagent while using 37% fewer subagent tokens. The manager needs skill at managing more than it needs sheer size, which is the gap Matryoshka Agent closes by training for the role: its Qwen3-4B orchestrator reaches orchestration performance comparable to o4-mini.
  • Do not read cost as a proxy for orchestration quality: ClawArena’s 100× cost spread against a sub-4× score spread says the expensive model is not reliably the better manager.

Possible future developments

Four lines of work are active.

Training the recursion instead of prompting it. Everything above treats the pattern as a wrapper around a model that was never trained for it. The RLM authors post-trained one small model on distilled RLM trajectories, and RLM-Qwen3-8B improved on the base Qwen3-8B by a median of 28% while running its trajectories more efficiently. Reinforcement learning on a 64K-token, two-needle split then generalized to a 1M-token, eight-needle split [1]. If that holds up at scale, “how to interact with your own input” becomes a trainable behavior in the same way chain-of-thought reasoning did.

Constraining the recursion instead of trusting it. The freedom that makes an RLM strong also makes it unverifiable. Arbitrary generated code has no termination guarantee and no cost bound, the same complaint the paper’s own limitations section makes about exploding sub-call costs. λ-RLM replaces free-form code generation with a typed runtime grounded in λ-calculus. It draws on a fixed set of combinators that have been verified ahead of time, and calls the model only on bounded leaf subproblems. The authors report termination and closed-form cost bounds, wins in 29 of 36 model-task comparisons against a standard RLM, and latency cut by up to 4.1× [20]. Whether the field prefers guarantees or freedom here is open.

Orchestration as code, in products. Dynamic workflows moved the plan out of the context window and into a script a user can read, diff, save, and rerun. That is a different artifact from a prompt: a plan you can inspect and edit before it runs, rather than a decomposition you reconstruct from a transcript afterward.

Asynchrony. Both literatures name the same missing piece. Anthropic notes that its lead agents run subagents one batch at a time, so the system waits on the slowest one and the lead cannot redirect a subagent already in progress [4]. The RLM authors list blocking sub-calls and absent prefix caching as their main implementation debt [1], [6]. Fixing this is engineering rather than research, and it changes the cost curve for both.

Zhang posed this as a contest between human-designed and model-chosen decomposition. That is not the question a year of results left open, because both approaches now let a model choose. The results settled the medium instead: a decomposition the model writes as code beats one it types out in prose, on the tasks measured so far. They left open how much freedom that code should get, and how much of it needs a type system, a permission model, or a cost bound around it before anyone puts it near production.
